articles.title: Judge rules Trump administration violated the First Amendment in fight against ICE-tracking
articles.summary: ICE Sightings - Chicago Land and Eyes Up won a preliminary injunction against the Trump administration for violating their First Amendment rights.
articles.body: Jorge L. Alonso, a federal district court judge for the Northern District of Illinois, said that the Trump Administration violated the First Amendment when it pressured Facebook and Apple to remove ICE-tracking groups and apps. Judge Alonso granted the plaintiffs, Kassandra Rosado, who runs the ICE Sightings – Chicagoland Facebook group, and Kreisau Group, the developers of Eyes Up, a preliminary injunction. Judge Alonso cited a unanimous Supreme Court decision from a 2024 case that pitted the NRA against the former superintendent of the New York Department of Financial Services, Maria Vullo. In that case, the court ruled that “[g]overnment officials cannot attempt to coerce private parties in order to punish or suppress views that the government disfavors,” when Vullo pressured companies to end their business relationships with the NRA. Alonso’s decision continues, saying, “Here, [Pam] Bondi and [Kristi] Noem did exactly that. They reached out to Facebook and Apple and demanded, rather than requested, that Facebook and Apple censor Plaintiff’s speech.” In the case of the ICE Sightings Facebook group, then Attorney General Pam Bondi bragged on X that an unnamed group “being used to dox and target” ICE agents had been taken down after the DOJ reached out to Meta. Eyes Up, ICEBlock, Red Dot, and other similar apps have been removed from app stores as well, following pressure from the DOJ and public threats of prosecution, including of CNN for simply reporting on the app’s existence. It’s likely that the government will appeal this decision, and the fight will continue. But the unanimous nature of the precedent set by the Supreme Court in 2024 suggests the Trump administration is facing an uphill battle.

articles.title: Jumbo Fed rate-hike warning sends shock waves after inflation surprise
articles.summary: Fed officials signal a more aggressive approach to interest rates amid hotter October CPI inflation.
articles.body:
Today's economic news is short but decidedly not sweet.

Gasoline prices may be easing, but American households are still paying more for groceries, healthcare, and other everyday expenses.

Now, a hotter-than-expected October inflation report has put a potentially much bigger Federal Reserve interest-rate increase on your kitchen table just in time for the holidays.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a 50-basis-point (0.5%) rate hike should be considered at the December policymaking meeting.

And Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan also warned that Fed officials may need to move faster and deliver at least two additional increases beginning next month to get inflation under control.

For Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, the stakes are growing. Six months into his leadership, the U.S. central bank's credibility as an inflation fighter is facing a major test.

Following months of waiting for economic data to confirm what American consumers and businesses have known and experienced firsthand — that prices are simply too damn high — the Fed heads into its final meeting of the year Dec. 8-9.

In light of political and economic pressures, it faces a stark choice: increase short-term interest rates to restore its anti-inflation credibility or risk letting price pressures spiral further out of reach.

"(The) Fed is losing its inflation-fighting credibility. Consumers who rely mostly on wages, not their stock portfolios, are paying the price,'' Diane Swonk, chief economist and managing director at KPMG, posted on LinkedIn.

Waller calls for bold action from the Fed on inflation

And those rate hikes could be massive if inflation continues to broaden away from supply shocks and into other sectors, as shown in the hotter-than-expected October Consumer Price Index at 0.4%, up from the 0.3% estimate, CNBC reported.

In October, food, energy, healthcare, recreation, medical care, motor vehicle insurance, and household furnishings all ticked up from the September readout. This is in part due to the geopolitical impact of diesel prices slamming the supply chain, causing businesses to pass along the pain.

Waller, speaking in London on Nov. 10 hours before the CPI release, upped the hawkish tone of the projected tightening cycle and said policymakers needed to take bold action if inflation came in hotter than the consensus forecast, which it did.

"In that case, I believe a 50-basis-point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take,'' Waller said in prepared remarks.

articles.title: Voo atrasado ou cancelado: veja quais são os direitos dos passageiros | G1
articles.standfirst: Passageiros podem exigir reembolso, hospedagem, alimentação e transporte; Anac reforça que suporte deve ser imediato.
articles.summary: Passageiro pode exigir reembolso, hospedagem, alimentação e transporte; Anac reforça que suporte deve ser imediato. País paralisou aeroportos e já afeta voos com origem no Brasil.
articles.body:
A Administração Federal de Aviação dos Estados Unidos (FAA, na sigla em inglês) paralisou todos os aeroportos dos Estados Unidos, nesta sexta-feira (13), por motivos de segurança após um problema de comunicação que afeta os centros de controle de tráfego aéreo. Voos com origem no Brasil já sofrem os impactos.

Os passageiros possuem uma série de direitos quando um um voo é cancelado ou atrasado, por qualquer motivo. As companhias aéreas são obrigadas a oferecer assistência aos passageiros.

Dependendo do caso, o cliente pode pedir reembolso ou ter direito a hospedagem, alimentação e acesso à internet, segundo a Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil (Anac).

O especialista em Direito Aeronáutico Felipe Bonsenso lembra que a lei exige apoio imediato, mesmo quando o atraso ou cancelamento não é culpa direta da empresa.

"Todos os passageiros devem procurar imediatamente as companhias aéreas e também podem recorrer à Justiça em busca de indenizações, em caso de perdas de eventos ou reuniões, por exemplo", diz.

O que a empresa deve fazer em caso de atraso ou cancelamento?

Segundo a resolução 400 da Anac, a companhia deve avisar o passageiro assim que souber do atraso ou cancelamento. Além disso, ela precisa adotar outras medidas:

manter o passageiro informado , a cada 30 minutos, sobre a previsão de partid a;

oferecer assistência gratuita de acordo com o tempo de espera;

garantir reacomodação, reembolso integral ou transporte alternativo , quando o atraso for maior que 4 horas ou em caso de cancelamento. A opção deve ser escolhida pelo passageiro .

Em caso de atraso, a assistência varia conforme o tempo de espera:

a partir de 1 hora: comunicação (internet, telefone ou outros meios);

a partir de 2 horas: alimentação (voucher ou refeição);

a partir de 4 horas: hospedagem (em caso de pernoite no aeroporto) e transporte . Se o voo for na cidade de residência do passageiro, a empresa pode oferecer apenas o transporte até a casa e de volta ao aeroporto.

Passageiros com Necessidade de Assistência Especial (Pnae) e seus acompanhantes têm direito a hospedagem em qualquer situação.

Um passageiro passa diante de um painel que exibe voos atrasados ​​dentro do terminal, após a Administração Federal de Aviação (FAA) dos EUA determinar uma suspensão nacional das decolagens "devido a circunstâncias extraordinárias e por motivos de segurança". A medida ocorreu na sequência de um relato anterior da agência sobre graves problemas nas comunicações de controle de tráfego aéreo no Aeroporto Internacional John F. Kennedy, em Nova York, EUA. — Foto: Angelina Katsanis/Reuters

Se a companhia aérea não oferecer as assistências, isso é considerado um descumprimento do contrato de transporte aéreo , segundo a Anac.

O passageiro deve primeiro procurar os canais de atendimento da empresa. Se não resolver, pode registrar reclamação na plataforma Consumidor.gov.br, usada pelo governo federal.

As queixas registradas nesse canal ajudam a Anac a identificar falhas e reforçar a fiscalização.

Caso o passageiro tenha prejuízos maiores, como a perda de uma entrevista de emprego ou de um casamento, pode pedir indenização além do reembolso. Para isso, deve acionar o Procon.

Se ainda assim ele se sentir insatisfeito, o caminho pode ser a Justiça, que seria o último recurso.

Além da resolução 400 da Anac, o Código de Defesa do Consumidor (CDC) também garante indenização por danos patrimoniais ou morais. Especialistas dizem que ele pode ser utilizado pelos passageiros que se sentirem prejudicados.

“No caso de cancelamento de voo, o artigo 14 do CDC estabelece que o prestador de serviço responde pelos danos que causa ao consumidor”, diz o advogado Rodrigo Alvim, especialista em direito do passageiro e do consumidor.

articles.summary: Winter is coming.

The Dow was up about 800 points. The S&P 500 was up 1.8%. On Fox Business, host Stuart Varney told viewers to take a look at their screens. "It's Monday morning. You like this stuff," he said (1).

But his guest, market expert Jeff Sica, was looking past the morning's rally. He had his eye on a decision that was still weeks away.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 5 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Gold has overtaken U.S. Treasuries as central banks' top reserve asset. Get Goldco's 2026 Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free

Varney brought up the inflation report due the next morning and suggested it might tempt the Fed to raise interest rates. Sica, CEO of Circle Squared Alternative Investments, cut straight to it.

"Stuart, not only are they tempted; they will raise interest rates," Sica said. "They're going to raise interest rates in December."

Sica pointed to Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's comments at Jackson Hole that Fed policy was not overly restrictive. Referring to the Fed's inflation target, Sica said, "He wants that 2%. We are not there yet. He is not going to back down. He is going to raise interest rates."

The Fed held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4% in October.

Its next meeting begins Dec. 8, with a decision due Dec. 9. And the inflation report (2) that landed after the interview gave officials more to think about. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October from the previous month, while core inflation, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% for a third straight month.

Hours before the numbers came out, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said (3) he was leaning toward a 25-basis-point increase in December.

He also said a 50-basis-point hike should be considered if monthly core inflation came in at 0.3% or higher. It came in right at that threshold. The committee still has to vote, but one member has already put a bigger move on the table.

While Sica expects the Fed to raise rates, he doubts a hike will do much about the prices that prompted it in the first place.

"I think it's going to be completely ineffective. I think it's going to hurt the economy," Sica said. "I think it's especially going to hurt all this debt and this wall of refinances."

He called the approach "an ill-conceived agenda considering where I think inflation is coming from."

articles.title: FDA issues recall for honey dietary supplement over undeclared ED ingredient
articles.summary: “The recall was initiated after FDA laboratory testing identified undeclared tadalafil,” the notice said.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A California-based company has recalled its honey dietary supplement after an undeclared ingredient used to treat erectile dysfunction was discovered in its products.

Eros Apothecary said its Candy Power For Man Organic Honey product contained tadalafil, according to a notice issued by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration .

“The recall was initiated after FDA laboratory testing identified undeclared tadalafil,” the notice said.

“Consumers should stop using Candy Power For Man immediately and dispose of any remaining product,” it continued.

The FDA said the product was sold on eBay between April 27 and July 20, and came in yellow and orange packaging.

Anyone who has experienced health issues after using the product should consult their healthcare provider, the notice stated.

articles.title: DJ Khaled shares he lost 90 pounds with help of GLP-1 drug
articles.summary: In October 2025, Khaled experienced a health scare at a concert, which led to a lifestyle change.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — DJ Khaled shared the reason why he took control of his health.

The producer revealed he lost 90 pounds since last year with the help of the weight loss drug Wegovy.

“The motivation was there, the inspiration was there, working out and trying to eat better, but I needed help,” he told People magazine . “We live for our kids, and our kids make us live. So, I have to do my part.”

Khaled admitted he had to “keep it real” with himself about his weight and spoke to a doctor about taking a GLP-1 .

The “All I Do is Win” performer began his weight loss journey between 295 and 300 pounds and now weighs between 200 and 212 pounds, he told People.

In October 2025, Khaled experienced a health scare at a concert, which led to a lifestyle change.

“There’s a part of my show where I get on my knees and give thanks and show my gratitude,” Khaled said. “So, I get on my knees … but I remember I couldn’t really get up.”

He noted, “One of my friends was coming to me like, ‘Yo, you were breathing hard.’ Then, 10 minutes later, somebody else told me the same thing.

“I said, alright, hold up. … I gotta step my game up. I gotta get my mind right. We can’t have this,” the artist added.

articles.title: Android TV box malware found in 1.3M devices
articles.summary: Google says Videostrong deliberately installed backdoor malware in over 1.3 million Android TV boxes, turning them into a botnet for criminals.
articles.body: You buy a streaming box, plug it into your television and connect it to Wi-Fi. A few minutes later, you're watching your favorite show. Everything seems perfectly normal. But what if that little box has been secretly working for criminals since the day you brought it home? That's the alarming discovery behind a massive Android TV box malware operation involving more than 1.3 million devices worldwide. According to a Nov. 2 report from Google's Threat Intelligence Group, investigators concluded with high confidence that a device manufacturer deliberately installed hidden software inside streaming hardware. That backdoor gave outsiders remote access without the owners knowing. And here's what makes this particularly concerning. The malware was built directly into the devices, and some affected products made it through Google's own security certification process. In other words, buyers could do everything right and still end up with compromised hardware. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. CHEAP ANDROID PHONES FOUND WITH MALWARE ALREADY INSTALLED Google uncovers malware hiding inside Android TV boxes Google says the operation involved Videostrong Technology, a China-based company that manufactures Android-powered devices for different brands. According to investigators, Videostrong developed and installed malicious software called XCPE. Google assesses with high confidence that the company deliberately operated the backdoor for financial gain. The software allowed remote operators to maintain access to devices long after customers purchased them. According to Google, Videostrong sold access to compromised devices to criminal affiliates, who installed additional malware and turned those products into part of a botnet. That's a network of infected devices controlled remotely without their owners' permission. Researchers identified more than 1.3 million affected devices across the globe. Most were Android TV streaming boxes, although the operation also reached other types of connected hardware. And many people using these products had no idea anything was wrong. What criminals were doing with infected streaming boxes While people were watching television, hidden software could be working behind the scenes for someone else. One of the biggest operations involved residential proxy networks. These services allow someone to route their internet activity through another person's home connection. That means a criminal could use your internet address to make suspicious online activity appear to originate from your household. Think about that for a moment. Someone you've never encountered could be using your internet connection without your permission, while your streaming box continues playing Netflix or YouTube. Google also found malware capable of generating fake advertising activity. Some modules secretly loaded ads or simulated interactions to generate revenue for the operators. Other capabilities were more invasive. Researchers observed operators capturing screenshots, injecting keystrokes and collecting sensitive account information from compromised devices. They could also install additional software remotely. And because much of this activity happened in the background, users might never see an obvious warning. 5 WORRISOME PRIVACY CLAUSES HIDDEN IN SMART HOME DEVICES How the Android TV malware bypassed Google's security Normally, manufacturers must pass Google's compatibility and security checks before shipping certified Android devices with Google's services. However, Google says Videostrong found a way around those protections. The company allegedly concealed malicious software during testing. The backdoor then loaded additional malicious code after the device's first startup, exploiting a gap in Google's review process. Even more concerning, the malware could disable Google Play Protect app verification. That's one of Android's built-in defenses against harmful applications. The backdoor also had staying power. Researchers discovered that XCPE was embedded in the device's firmware, the software responsible for basic hardware operations. If someone removed the visible malware package, the system could reinstall it after a reboot. So even a factory reset might leave the underlying infection intact. Which Android TV boxes are affected? This is probably the first question people will ask after hearing about this investigation. Unfortunately, Google has not released a complete consumer-friendly list of every infected retail product. However, cybersecurity company Synthient published its own investigation identifying specific hardware and model names connected to the operation. Confirmed infected streaming box Researchers purchased and examined a MECOOL KM9PRO Max Android TV streaming box in late 2025. They found the XCPE backdoor preinstalled under the package name com.oemservice. The tested device used firmware version C1.0.8_20250325, according to Synthient's technical documentation. This identifies the specific research sample, although it does not establish that every unit running that version is infected. Other device models identified by researchers Synthient also published model identifiers observed in the wider botnet. These include KM9PRO_MAX, KM9PRO, KM2PLUSDELUXE, KM2PLUS, KM7PLUS, KT1, IPx1, IPx3, Q96MAX and TX3MINI. These identifiers appeared in data associated with the malicious operation. However, researchers explicitly warn that a matching model name alone cannot confirm that an individual device is compromised. You can review Synthient's published device model list at github.com/synthient/public-research/blob/main/2026/11/Videostrong/README.md to compare it with your own hardware. The investigation also identified infections in Android-powered karaoke machines, digital signage equipment and some telehealth devices. Google says the malware appeared across many models and brands over several years. And that's why checking the exact product you own is so important. The retail brand on the box may differ from the company responsible for manufacturing its hardware or firmware. Google shuts down the XCPE botnet and bans manufacturer Google worked with Japan's National Police Agency and several cybersecurity companies to dismantle the XCPE operation. Google took legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control infected devices and install malware. The company also pursued legal action against command-and-control domains associated with more than a dozen additional malware families. According to Google, those additional actions were expected to sever criminal access to at least 10 million other compromised devices. That estimate involves malware networks beyond the 1.3 million devices identified in the XCPE operation. Google also cut ties with Videostrong and banned the company, along with future subsidiaries and affiliates, from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software to other certified vendors. The company says it has also strengthened its security review process to better detect similar threats, including improvements to how it verifies the integrity of firmware on certified Android TV devices. That's encouraging news, but there's an important catch. Disrupting the servers used to control malware doesn't automatically remove malicious firmware from devices already sitting in people's homes. For owners of affected hardware, that leaves an important question about whether their devices can ever be trusted again. How to protect yourself from Android TV box malware Now, before you start unplugging every streaming device in your house, understand that Google has not suggested every Android TV or Google TV product is compromised. However, this investigation offers a good reason to take a closer look at the equipment connected to your home network. 1) Check your streaming box's brand and model Start by identifying the exact make and model of your streaming device. Look on the underside of the box, its original packaging or the device information screen in Settings. Compare that information with Synthient's list of observed models. If your device matches a listed model, investigate further. Remember, a model match alone does not confirm an infection. If you own the MECOOL KM9PRO Max examined by researchers, take the warning seriously and consider replacing it. 2) Disconnect a device you believe is infected If you have strong reason to suspect your streaming box contains malicious firmware, disconnect it from Wi-Fi or unplug it entirely. Contact the manufacturer or retailer about a verified clean firmware update, replacement or refund. Synthient recommends permanently removing affected devices from use because they may contain additional malware. Don't assume a factory reset will solve the problem. The XCPE backdoor was designed to reinstall itself. 3) Check Google Play Protect certification On devices with the Google Play Store, open the Play Store, tap your profile icon and select Settings > About to check the Play Protect certification status. You can also open Play Protect from your profile menu to review security scanning. However, certification alone cannot guarantee a device is free of malware. Some devices associated with this investigation passed Google's certification checks. A certified label offers an additional layer of reassurance, but it cannot guarantee that a device is free of malware. 4) Avoid suspicious streaming apps and cheap TV boxes Be cautious about streaming products promising unlimited premium channels or paid entertainment for a suspiciously low one-time price. The FBI has previously warned about questionable streaming hardware that arrives with malware or installs it during setup. Stick with reputable manufacturers that provide regular security updates. Also, avoid installing streaming applications from unofficial websites or unknown app marketplaces. 5) Keep your home router updated and secure Your router connects your streaming equipment to the rest of your home network. Make sure its firmware is current and review the list of connected devices for unfamiliar equipment. If your router supports a separate guest or smart-home network, consider placing streaming boxes and other connected gadgets there. That can help limit their access to your personal computers and other sensitive devices. If you discover an infected device, disconnect it before changing your Wi-Fi password. A password change alone will not remove malware already embedded in the box. 6) Watch for unusual internet activity Check your router's activity logs or connected-device information if those features are available. Unexplained bandwidth consumption or unfamiliar network connections can be warning signs, although they do not prove a device has malware. Keep in mind that an infected streaming box may show no obvious symptoms. Normal performance doesn't guarantee that the hardware is secure. 7) Protect accounts connected to your streaming device If you've signed into streaming services or a Google account on a device you believe was compromised, change those passwords using a trusted computer or phone. Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) where available. Also, review your account activity for unfamiliar sign-ins. Google observed operators collecting sensitive information from compromised devices, so protecting those accounts is a sensible precaution. 8) Use strong antivirus protection on compatible devices Strong antivirus software can help protect your computers and smartphones from malicious downloads and other threats. Keep those protections enabled, especially when dealing with unfamiliar applications. However, traditional antivirus software on your computer won't remove a backdoor embedded in a streaming box's firmware. If the box itself is compromised, disconnecting and replacing it may be the safest solution. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com 9) Be careful with apps that pay you to share internet bandwidth Some services offer compensation in exchange for allowing others to use your unused internet connection. Google specifically warns that these arrangements can expose devices and home networks to additional security risks. Before installing any bandwidth-sharing or proxy application, understand exactly who can access your connection and what activity they may conduct through it. Kurt's key takeaways What really gets my attention about this investigation is how little someone would have needed to do to become a victim. You could buy a streaming box from an online retailer, connect it to your television and end up with malware that was already installed before you opened the package. And there's another part of this story I find particularly frustrating. Some affected devices made it through Google's certification process. People rely on those certifications because they assume someone has checked the hardware for security problems. In this case, that trust was exploited. Google deserves credit for working with investigators to disrupt the operation. But I think the bigger responsibility starts with manufacturers and the companies selling these products. If a company puts compromised hardware into someone's home, it should be held accountable for fixing the problem. For me, the takeaway is pretty simple. Know what you're connecting to your home network. Stick with brands that have a solid record of security updates. And if researchers confirm that a streaming box contains malicious firmware, I wouldn't keep using it simply because the picture on the television still looks fine. If a streaming box can pass Google's security checks and still arrive with hidden malware, should manufacturers be required to recall compromised devices and compensate customers? articles.title: Tanker collides with riverboat on Mississippi River at Port of New Orleans
articles.summary: The American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage riverboat was docked at the port when it was struck by the Atlantic Asphalt tanker Friday afternoon.
articles.body:
NEW ORLEANS ( WGNO /NEXSTAR) – At least 180 passengers and crew members were rescued Friday after a tanker collided with a cruise ship on the Mississippi River, near the Port of New Orleans.

The American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage riverboat was docked at the port when it was struck by the Atlantic Asphalt tanker Friday afternoon. The collision caused the boat to partially submerge.

New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said that 32 people were taken to the hospital, none with critical injuries. Moreno called the rescue “a miracle on the Mississippi.”

“American Cruise Lines can confirm that our riverboat, American Heritage was involved in a collision while it was docked in New Orleans,” a spokesperson for the company said Friday. “We are in close coordination with the U.S. Coast Guard and local authorities. Guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved.”

Video shared to social media, meanwhile, appeared to show the American Heritage riverboat falling to one side, rapidly taking on water. Other images later showed the vessel completely on its side, mostly submerged. Rescue workers could also be seen pulling people to another vessel from the water.

The type of tanker that struck the ship specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic. It is not immediately clear whether the ship was carrying any materials when the crash occurred.

The cruise ship was built in 2015 and originally known as the Queen of the Mississippi before being rebranded as the American Heritage. It is five stories and can hold up to 150 passengers. The paddlewheeler was just finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi when the accident occurred.

Port of New Orleans reported that Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard and emergency medical personnel all responded to the emergency.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Navy removed naval destroyer commander deployed to Middle East
articles.summary: The U.S. Navy in late September removed a commander of the naval destroyer that was deployed to the Middle East in support of military operations against Iran because of “loss of confidence” after she had been in the job for less than a year, The Hill has learned. Commander of Carrier Strike Group 10, Rear…
articles.body:
The U.S. Navy in late September removed a commander of the naval destroyer that was deployed to the Middle East in support of military operations against Iran because of “loss of confidence” after she had been in the job for less than a year, The Hill has learned.

Commander of Carrier Strike Group 10, Rear Adm. Todd F. Cimicata, relieved Cmdr. Caitlin Cunningham of her duties as USS Michael Murphy’s commanding officer on Sept. 27, a Navy official told The Hill on Friday.

Cunningham began her role as the skipper of USS Michael Murphy, an Arleigh Burke-class Aegis guided-missile destroyer, in late October last year before the ship embarked on an 11-month deployment, which ended this week .

The destroyer departed Pearl Harbor on Dec. 1, 2025, operating alongside flagship Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln.

No additional information was available about Cunningham’s removal, which was reported earlier by USNI News .

The USS Michael Murphy helped enforce the U.S. naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, operating in the north Arabian Sea and Gulf of Oman.

“The Sailors of Michael Murphy demonstrated unmatched grit, professionalism and warfighting excellence during this deployment,” Cmdr. David Nicolas, Michael Murphy’s commanding officer, said in a press release . “Whether defeating incoming air and surface threats or leading operations through contested choke points, this crew never hesitated.”

“They answered every call of our nation, defended our allies, and lived up to the heroic namesake,” Nicolas said. “I could not be prouder of this crew.”

articles.title: Kevin Hassett Says He Will Remain as Trump Economic Adviser
articles.summary: National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett denied a report that he plans to depart his post in the coming weeks.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett denied a report that he plans to depart his post in the coming weeks.

"Not true," Hassett said in a text message Friday when asked about the report on his impending departure.

Semafor reported earlier that Hassett is expected leave his role as President Donald Trump's top economic adviser. The news outlet said his potential replacements include Scott Bessent, who would retain his role as Treasury secretary, and Bessent's counselor David Zervos.

Hassett said he joked about the report with the president on Friday afternoon. A White House official also said the report has no factual basis, adding that Hassett is a key member of Trump's economic team and will continue working to advance his policies.

Republican losses in the midterm elections have intensified speculation about a shake-up of the president's team. Days after the midterms, Trump's chief of staff Susie Wiles left and was replaced by Stephen Miller. That move is expected to lead to further changes on the president's staff.

Trump himself has said he expects some turnover among his advisers.

As NEC director, Hassett is responsible for coordinating economic policy across the federal government. A frequent presence on television, Hassett is staunch defender of the president's policies, including his sweeping use of tariff powers, as Trump moved in his second term to reshape US manufacturing and ties with trading partners.

articles.title: US government grounds all flights across the United States 'due to extraordinary circumstances' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A spokesperson for the FAA told TechCrunch that it issued the ground stop "following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers," which manage the airspace across the United States.
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday afternoon that it has grounded all flights across the United States due to “extraordinary circumstances” and issues related to safety.

The FAA’s website said the cause is an “equipment outage.” The site itself was down for a brief period at the time of publication, with a note that the website was “experiencing technical difficulties.”

Per an alert sent by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center , or ATCSCC, the FAA said the ground stop means that aircraft cannot take off from departure gates. The message said that the disruption was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” but did not specify further. The alert was not visible on the ATCSCC website at press time.

The alert stated that all departing flights must remain on the ground “until further notice.” Inbound international flights will be “managed on a case-by-case basis,” it said.

A spokesperson for the FAA told TechCrunch that it issued the ground stop “following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” which manage the airspace across the United States.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a post on X : “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”

It’s not clear what caused the ongoing FAA equipment outage. The outage comes in the same week that the administration rolled out an AI-powered tool for air traffic controllers to save aircraft flight time and fuel costs — though it’s unclear if the ongoing outage is related.

Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that there is “no indication yet that this was a nefarious act,” but warned that the recovery “is going to take some time.”

Updated with comment from the FAA, and remarks from Homeland Security.

articles.title: Fed says it's monitoring the data center build-out for risks to the financial system
articles.summary: The Fed says that in the event of a downturn in artificial intelligence, the defaults on debt could be larger than current balance sheets suggest.
articles.body:
The Federal Reserve is closely monitoring leverage in the rapid data center build-out, noting that in the event of a downturn in artificial intelligence, the defaults on debt could be larger than current balance sheets suggest , according to a report on financial stability released Friday.

Initially, hyperscalers self-funded data centers, with debt issuance having risen to more than $680 billion as of October — a fivefold increase from $130 billion in all of 2023. But now the composition of the debt being issued is evolving from mostly corporate bonds to a combination of public and private debt and structured credit.

In addition, large technology firms are rapidly increasing future lease commitments, backstop guarantees provided to other firms, and other complex and contingent obligations.

A dynamic of circular financing is taking hold that echoes the 2008 financial crisis in which there was mounting debt off firms' balance sheets. The evidence suggests AI firms' economic exposure in the event of a downturn could be larger than their current balance sheets would suggest.

Hyperscaler firms often enter into long-term leases for data center capacity with third-party data center developers. These leases are then used by the third-party developers to secure financing for construction. In addition, graphics processing unit (GPU) makers often provide a guaranteed residual value of the GPU collateral to support purchases of their GPUs by advanced computing technology or large language model (LLM) firms. These debt financings that link hyperscalers and GPU designers with smaller firms are often supplemented by equity investments from the hyperscalers and GPU designers, creating a "circular financing" dynamic.

That's deepening the connection between large hyperscalers and smaller, riskier companies with less access to credit.

The Fed estimates future leases and backstop guarantees for data center build-outs are about $3 trillion now. It says cash outflows for capital expenditures suggest that the pace of the current cycle's investment may surpass that of the 1990s telecom cycle relatively soon.

At the same time, asset valuations across asset classes, from stocks to corporate bonds and real estate, are elevated, and hedge funds have the most leverage since 2013.

Follow Jennifer Schonberger on X @Jenniferisms and on Instagram .

articles.title: Oriximiná aplica multa imediata por descarte irregular de lixo | G1
articles.standfirst: Nova lei permite autuação eletrônica no momento em que a infração for identificada. Responsáveis também poderão ser identificados por meio de denúncias.
articles.summary: Nova lei em Oriximiná permite multa imediata por descarte irregular de lixo com uso de fotos e QR Code, além de cobrança pelos custos de limpeza da prefeitura.
articles.body:
Oriximiná passa a aplicar multa imediata para quem descartar lixo irregularmente nas ruas — Foto: Prefeitura de Oriximiná/Divulgação

A Prefeitura de Oriximiná , no oeste do Pará, começou a aplicar novas regras para punir quem descartar lixo irregularmente em ruas, terrenos e outros espaços públicos. Com a Lei Municipal nº 9.700/2026, a multa poderá ser aplicada imediatamente após a identificação da infração, sem a necessidade de uma notificação prévia para que o responsável retire os resíduos.

A medida faz parte da Operação Final de Ano – Campanha Cidade Limpa, apresentada durante uma reunião de alinhamento realizada na quinta-feira (12). A ação envolve as secretarias municipais de Planejamento, Eficiência Governamental e Infraestrutura, além do Departamento de Código de Postura.

Campanha busca reduzir descarte irregular em Oriximiná — Foto: SEINFRA/Limpeza Urbana

Uma das novidades da legislação é a implantação do Auto de Infração Eletrônico (AIE). O sistema permitirá que os fiscais registrem a irregularidade por meio de fotografias, localização geográfica e validação por QR Code.

Com isso, a multa poderá ser emitida no momento em que o descarte irregular for constatado. A fiscalização também poderá identificar os responsáveis a partir de denúncias feitas pela população.

Segundo o secretário municipal de Planejamento e Administração, Bosco Almeida, a nova legislação acaba com a etapa de notificação inicial que concedia prazo para a retirada do lixo antes da aplicação da penalidade.

O secretário de Obras Públicas e Habitação, Gelzadac Vitor, também reforçou que a população já passou por um período de conscientização e que as multas poderão ser aplicadas assim que a infração for identificada.

A medida integra a Operação Final de Ano – Campanha Cidade Limpa, apresentada durante reunião de alinhamento realizada na manhã da quinta-feira (12) — Foto: SEMOPH/Divulgação

Quem receber uma autuação terá 15 dias para apresentar defesa, presencialmente ou por meio eletrônico, junto à secretaria responsável.

A lei prevê ainda desconto de 10% para quem pagar a multa até a data de vencimento indicada na guia. Mesmo com o pagamento antecipado, o cidadão poderá contestar a penalidade. Caso a defesa ou o recurso sejam aceitos, o valor pago poderá ser devolvido ou compensado.

Se a defesa for negada pelo secretário municipal responsável, o cidadão poderá recorrer ao prefeito no prazo de 10 dias. Não será necessário pagar a multa ou fazer depósito prévio para apresentar o recurso.

Prefeitura poderá cobrar custos de limpeza

A legislação também estabelece medidas para quem deixar de cumprir determinações da fiscalização, como a limpeza de terrenos e a retirada de entulhos.

Se o responsável não realizar o serviço dentro do prazo estabelecido, a Prefeitura poderá executar a limpeza diretamente ou contratar uma empresa para fazer o trabalho.

Os custos com mão de obra, transporte e equipamentos serão cobrados do responsável, com acréscimo de 20% referente à taxa de administração. Após receber a notificação de ressarcimento, ele terá 15 dias para contestar os valores ou o serviço realizado.

A Operação Cidade Limpa busca reduzir o descarte irregular de resíduos e reforçar a fiscalização nos espaços públicos de Oriximiná.

De acordo com a Prefeitura, as equipes de limpeza urbana trabalham diariamente, inclusive aos domingos. A administração municipal orienta os moradores a respeitar os dias e horários da coleta de lixo e evitar o descarte de resíduos em ruas, terrenos e outros locais inadequados.

articles.title: Fed’s Jefferson Says Inflation Will Determine Rate Decisions
articles.summary: Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said inflation has become the most important measure for policymakers as they consider additional interest-rate h...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said inflation has become the most important measure for policymakers as they consider additional interest-rate hikes.

Recent economic activity and labor market conditions have been solid, while price pressures remained persistent, Jefferson said. Price data for October was consistent with well-above-target inflation, he said.

"Accordingly, I see the trajectory of inflation as providing the more important signal for determining the appropriate stance of monetary policy," Jefferson said in remarks prepared for a speech in San Diego, adding that policymakers should continue to watch incoming data in considering "further policy adjustments."

Jefferson capped a week of Fed speakers this week who cemented market expectations for an interest-rate increase in December by voicing sharp concerns over price pressures.

A number of other officials called for more rapid policy adjustments than they had previously, including Fed Governor Christopher Waller, who warned that a 50-basis-points move may be needed next month. A few others, however, like Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson, stuck with calls for a gradual pace of rate hikes.

Investors are expecting hikes in December and January, and another in either March or April, according to federal funds futures pricing.

In his speech, which was focused on technology and productivity, Jefferson said there's a risk that new technology upends the labor market by putting people out of work before they have an opportunity to retrain. That would force policymakers to asses how much of the increase in joblessness was structural — resulting from a persistent mismatch between workers' skills and employers' needs even with strong economic growth.

"Monetary policy can affect cyclical conditions, like a temporary downturn in employment and spending, but it cannot address the structural factors that determine long-run rates of employment," Jefferson cautioned.

It's also possible the technology boom causes the neutral rate of interest — one that is neither slowing nor stimulating the economy — to rise, Jefferson said. Higher productivity growth that spurs consumer spending and robust investment into the AI buildout may ultimately push the neutral rate higher.

articles.body:
The nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration Friday afternoon has impacted travel plans for college football teams scheduled to fly to their destinations.

Among teams impacted are four schools in the NCAA’s Big 12 Conference, Baylor University, Kansas State University, University of Utah and Arizona State University; three in the Big Ten — University of Minnesota, Purdue University and University of Washington; as well as the universities of Mississippi, Tennessee and Texas, ESPN reported Friday night.

Teams including Oregon State University, Boise State University, University of North Texas and University of Wyoming were also on flights that were either grounded or never left due to the stop, according to ESPN.

“The safety and well-being of student athletes, coaches, and team personnel remain out highest priority,” the NCAA’s Southeastern Conference wrote in a statement posted to social platform X.

Big 12 Conference, in a separate post to X, wrote it was “evaluating potential changes to Saturday’s football schedule.”

The nationwide grounding began at around 4 p.m. EST and continued into Friday evening. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote in a 4:16 p.m. post on social platform X made the order “following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”

The FAA lifted the stop at around 8:15 p.m. and airspace reopened, Duffy confirmed during a White House press briefing at around 8:30 p.m., though he clarified the return to normal flight operations is expected to be “slow.”

“It’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon,” Duffy said.

Duffy attributed the incident to an overload of data on routers, with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin adding the “public was never in danger in this process.”

articles.title: Duffy, Mullin call for $50B air travel ‘overhaul’ in fiery ground stop briefing
articles.summary: Trump administration officials reupped their calls for a multi-billion-dollar investment into updating the U.S.’s “incredibly old” air traffic control systems, calling out Congress for “[kicking] the can down the road” on improvements they argued could have prevented Friday night’s nationwide ground stop. “What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Transportation Secretary…
articles.body:
Trump administration officials reupped their calls for a multi-billion-dollar investment into updating the U.S.’s “incredibly old” air traffic control systems, calling out Congress for “[kicking] the can down the road” on improvements they argued could have prevented Friday night’s nationwide ground stop.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said during the Friday night briefing after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted the stoppage. “Let’s not do a patchwork, a fix to a system that’s critical for every single family.”

“I want $50 billion,” he said, noting President Trump had asked for $30 billion in the past. “Let’s finish this job: new hardware, new software, new telecommunication.”

Duffy in later September asked Congress for $30 billion to fund new technology, control towers and airport improvements across the country. The push came as the FAA began to roll out its Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories — or SMART — program, an AI tool designed to help air traffic controllers anticipate congestion and reduce delays.

The FAA issued the nationwide ground stop at around 4 p.m. EST Friday. The rare protocol was in place for nearly four hours. The agency’s last widespread stoppage, which lasted approximately 90 minutes, was in 2023 due to a contractor outage.

Prior to that, the lasted time the FAA halted all American air travel was on Sept. 11, 2001, in response to the terror attacks — which involved commercial plane hijackings.

During the briefing, Duffy said Friday’s incident was due to an overload of data on routers, with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin adding the “public was never in danger in this process.”

“Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data,” Duffy said. “They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those … routers. And because of that, we shut the system down.”

Mullin also said officials have “zero evidence” a cyber-attack led to the telecommunications issue, though he added federal authorities are still investigating the situation.

The stop was lifted at around 8:15 p.m. and airspace reopened, Duffy confirmed during the meeting, though he clarified the return to normal flight operations is expected to be “slow.”

“It’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon,” Duffy said.

Mullin echoed Duffy’s call for funding to build a new updated system, saying, “It has to be a complete overhaul of the system, which we estimate to be about $50 billion.”

“I think every member of Congress should say yes … every American, I guarantee you, would tell those members, ‘Yes, give President Trump — give Duffy the money. Let them finish this job so we don’t have to do a press conference at 8:30 at night ever again,'” Duffy said.

articles.body:
Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company behind a recently deployed Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) AI tool, denied any link to the nationwide ground stop issued Friday afternoon.

“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a 5:34 p.m. EST post to social platform X , while the stoppage was still in effect.

The nationwide grounding began Friday afternoon and lasted for around four hours. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote in a 4:16 p.m. post on social platform X the FAA made the order “following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”

The airspace was opened at around 8:15 p.m. and the stop was lifted, Duffy said during a White House briefing that began 15 minutes later. The secretary said the incident resulted from an overload of data on routers.

“Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data,” Duffy said. “They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those … routers. And because of that, we shut the system down.”

The FAA deployed the new Strategic Management of Airspace, Routing and Trajectories — or SMART — tool in September in Washington, D.C. The AI-powered system, which cost the Transportation Department $875 million , is meant to ingest real-time data as well as current and future weather conditions to recommend necessary flight path changes to air traffic controllers, Duffy said at the time.

During Friday’s briefing, the secretary asserted the SMART tool had nothing to do with the ground stop, saying the system “isn’t plugged in.”

“This is completely disconnected , and I love that some people have said this would be the root cause. By the way, if it was, I’ll tell you that, but this is not even plugged in,” he said. “So , there’s no possible way SMART would have impacted.”

Duffy also asked Congress for $50 billion to rebuild what he described as an “incredibly old” air traffic control system, aligning with his ongoing efforts to modernize U.S. air travel. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin echoed Duffy’s call, saying, “It has to be a complete overhaul of the system.”

In September, Duffy had asked the Congress for $30 billion to fund new technology, control towers and airport improvements across the country.

BEIJING, Nov 14 (Reuters) - China and the United States discussed tariff cuts, agricultural trade and other issues at ‌their first trade council meeting on Friday, China's Commerce ‌Ministry said on Saturday, days ahead of an expected leaders' meeting in Shenzhen ​next week.

"The two sides held candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on implementing the outcomes of previous China-US economic and trade talks, including tariffs, a reciprocal '$30 billion-for-$30 billion' tariff-cut arrangement, agricultural trade and other ‌issues of mutual concern," ⁠the ministry said.

It did not say whether any agreements were reached. Both sides will continue using ⁠the council to address trade concerns, expand cooperation and reduce outstanding issues, the ministry added.

Following a September summit between Presidents Xi Jinping ​and Donald ​Trump in Washington, the two ​sides proposed a $60 billion ‌package of reciprocal tariff cuts, including roughly $17 billion worth of US farm goods that China imported in 2024, but the plan has yet to be finalised.

Chinese purchases of US farm goods other than soybeans are on track to hit a seven-year low ‌this year, despite an agreement to ​buy $17 billion annually through 2028, a Reuters ​analysis of customs data ​showed earlier this month, underscoring persistent uncertainty over ‌the deal.

Beijing has repeatedly urged ​Washington to implement ​the $60 billion tariff-reduction deal, calling it a prerequisite for increasing purchases of US farm goods.

The White House said Trump ​will meet Xi ‌on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation ​forum in Shenzhen.

articles.title: Trump says the Iran war ‘effectively over.’ It’s still costing the US billions
articles.summary: President Trump this week declared the war in Iran “effectively over” militarily and “won” by the U.S. But he did so as American taxpayers are footing the bill for billions of dollars in operational costs to keep the country’s troops at the ready overseas. The war is no longer making top headlines, and firing between…
articles.body:
President Trump this week declared the war in Iran “effectively over” militarily and “won” by the U.S.

But he did so as American taxpayers are footing the bill for billions of dollars in operational costs to keep the country’s troops at the ready overseas.

The war is no longer making top headlines, and firing between the U.S. and Iran is not taking place on a daily basis.

Yet the U.S. has a large presense in the region and is effectively in a war posture, despite the president’s remarks, which come after a midterm shellacking for his party driven in part by voter unhappiness over the war.

“We won. Now the question is when we want to end. We must have a total victory. Not a 93 percent victory. It’s going to be total,” Trump said Wednesday in remarks during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery.

A few days prior in a surprise visit to the White House briefing room, Trump declared: “Iran militarily is effectively over. We’re just keeping it the status quo.”

Despite Trump’s remarks, the U.S. is spending millions on the Iran conflict.

The total cost of the fight as of Oct. 16 is estimated at $47.1 billion, including $38 billion accrued from when the war began on Feb. 28 up until the start of August, according to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO).

That means another $9 billion was added over the last three months or so, a relatively quiet period that underscores the costs to taxpayers. During that timeframe, the U.S. military reportedly only carrying out a handful of defensive strikes against the regime after it all but depleted its stockpiles of advanced munitions.

That’s $2 billion to $3 billion per month in continuing costs, meaning the war is approaching a $50 billion price tag, according to Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think tank.

She warned that those costs could escalate if there is an increase in fighting.

“The war is not over,” Yacoubian told The Hill. “If there is a spike in conflict, war costs will also spike.”

Trump this week indicated it’s unlikely he will order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the war continue positively.

“It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump told CNN in a phone interview on Sunday. “The answer is, highly unlikely ‌it’s going to be necessary.”

Talks between the two sides are taking place but appear shaky, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Wednesday accusing the U.S. of threatening to attack his country with America’s “mother of all bombs,” its largest non-nuclear weapon even as the U.S. pursues a peace deal.

The big cost for the U.S. comes from maintaining a naval blockade on Iran in the Strait of Hormuz.

Yacoubian described this as “a 24-7 operation that entails all sorts of costs related to diverting some ships, intercepting others, protecting friendly ones, not to mention U.S. force protection.”

“All of these elements have costs associated which is why the blockade could be difficult to sustain over an extended period,” she added.

Washington’s naval blockade of Iranian ports has now lasted more than 100 days, an undertaking that has cost considerable sums.

In the first week of November, the U.S. military maintained two aircraft carriers, 11 destroyers and a cruiser in the Arabian Sea, along with two destroyers in the Red Sea. Another three destroyers are operating under the U.S. Sixth Fleet in the Mediterranean Sea, according to the Institute for National Security Studies.

Alongside the blockade – which requires American ships to burn through fuel, food and other critical supplies for tens of thousands of service members – the United States has carried out limited, defensive strikes on Iranian targets should Tehran fire upon its aircraft or vessels.

The most recent such incident fell on Nov. 2, when U.S. warplanes struck an anti-aircraft site on Qeshm Island and another island in the Strait of Hormuz after Tehran fired a missile at an American aircraft.

Outside the everyday costs to fuel America’s war machine in the Middle East, the Pentagon has suffered more than $65 billion in estimated costs to repair or replace U.S. military facilities damaged or destroyed by Iranian attacks – something that hasn’t been factored into CBO estimates, according to Yacoubian.

The Trump administration is requesting up to $70 billion in emergency military spending to cover the costs of the Iran war and to pay for new weapons and personnel.

The president as of late has insisted U.S. allies in the Middle East will “pay” America’s bill for the conflict.

“Those countries that we’ve protected are going to pay us back any and all costs that we’ve had for the war,” the president said in an interview with CBS News that aired Sunday.

Outside of direct cost to the U.S. govenment, the continued chokehold of the Strait of Hormuz has kept fuel costs and the prices of other goods heightened for U.S. consumers, an issue that Republican lawmakers admit torpedoed their chances to keep control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections.

Case in point, America’s households are expected to face higher fuel costs this winter, with heating costs projected to average $1,002 across all fuels, up 7.1 percent from last winter, according to estimates from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association released this week.

Those who rely primarily on heating oil – more than 4 million households – will pay some $2,977 this winter, up roughly 70 percent from last year.

articles.title: Ford privacy promise raises questions about your car data
articles.summary: Ford's new privacy promise pledges not to sell driving data to insurers or brokers, but disabling connected car data sharing could cost you key features.
articles.body: Your car probably knows more about you than you realize. It can track where you drive, how fast you go and whether something under the hood needs attention. Depending on the vehicle, that information may also travel back to the manufacturer. And chances are, you haven't spent much time thinking about who gets to see it. Now, Ford wants to put those privacy concerns in the spotlight. On Nov. 2, the automaker announced a new Ford privacy promise designed to give drivers more transparency and control over their personal information. The company also says it won't sell data about how customers drive to insurance companies or data brokers. That sounds encouraging. But there's a catch worth understanding. Turning off certain data-sharing settings could also mean losing some of the connected features you've come to rely on. So how much privacy can you get without giving up the technology you paid for? Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS ARE TRACKING DRIVERS EVERYWHERE What is Ford's new privacy promise? Ford says its new privacy initiative will make it easier for drivers to understand what information their vehicles collect and how the company uses it. The automaker has also launched a dedicated data and privacy website where owners can learn about their options. The announcement centers on several commitments. Ford says it designs its products with privacy in mind and wants customers to have clearer information about their choices. It also promises to respect the privacy settings drivers select. Perhaps the biggest commitment involves what happens to driving information. Ford specifically says it does not sell data about how customers drive to insurance companies or data brokers. However, that promise does not mean Ford stops collecting connected vehicle data altogether. The company still uses information from equipped vehicles to operate services and improve its technology. Ford's chief privacy officer, Kristin Jones, explained to TechCrunch that the company wants to build greater trust by helping customers understand its data practices. The effort comes as Ford prepares to introduce more connected vehicles, including models built on its upcoming universal electric vehicle platform. Importantly, many of Ford's privacy controls already existed. The new initiative focuses on making those controls easier to understand and find. What information can your Ford collect? Modern Ford vehicles can generate a surprising amount of information. Exactly what gets collected depends on your model, its connected features and the privacy settings you select. For example, Ford says equipped connected vehicles may share information about: There are practical benefits to some of this sharing. Vehicle diagnostics can help identify maintenance problems earlier. Location information can support roadside assistance or help you find your parked car. Ford also says it may use connected vehicle data to improve future technologies. With your consent, certain information can support personalization and relevant offers. Still, your driving habits can reveal personal details about your daily routine. That's why understanding which settings are enabled deserves your attention. Why Ford's privacy promise comes at a critical time Ford's announcement follows increased scrutiny of how automakers handle customer information. On Oct. 29, a coalition of 36 attorneys general announced a $220 million settlement with General Motors over allegations involving drivers' personal information. The states alleged that GM collected and sold driving behavior and location data to third parties, including data brokers that supplied information to insurance companies. According to the state attorneys general, some insurers used that information when calculating insurance rates. The settlement requires GM to obtain affirmative, express consent before collecting or disclosing covered driving and location data. GM previously discontinued its Smart Driver program. The case shows why vehicle privacy has become such a sensitive issue. Drivers may agree to connected features without fully understanding how much information those systems collect. We've explored similar concerns in our CyberGuy article, Is it worth saving money to let a car insurance company track your every move? Insurance monitoring programs can offer savings, but drivers should understand what information they are agreeing to share. Against that backdrop, Ford's public commitment could help set expectations for how automakers handle sensitive driving information. The privacy tradeoff that could affect your Ford's features Ford says customers can turn off connected vehicle data sharing. However, doing so may affect some of the features that make newer vehicles convenient. Depending on your Ford model, equipment and which settings you disable, you could lose access to: The exact impact depends on which settings you disable and the technology installed in your vehicle. Turning off all vehicle connectivity can affect more features than changing individual data-sharing preferences. Some features can continue working even when connected vehicle data sharing is disabled. Ford says features such as Apple CarPlay and Android Auto compatibility can continue working without sharing connected vehicle data with Ford. Local Bluetooth connections and regular radio playback can also remain available. Of course, availability depends on your vehicle's equipment and software. Before turning anything off, check which services your particular Ford needs. Disabling one optional sharing preference does not automatically disable every connected feature. And remember, Apple CarPlay and Android Auto use smartphone technology. Your phone and its apps may have their own data collection settings that you'll want to review separately. How to change your Ford's privacy settings Ford gives owners several ways to review their data-sharing preferences. You can manage vehicle connectivity through the car's touchscreen. The Ford app and your online Ford account provide additional controls for certain uses of your information. Check privacy settings inside your Ford Start with the vehicle parked safely. Ford recommends that owners of vehicles built in 2018 or later review their connected vehicle settings. Menu names and available controls vary by Ford model and infotainment system. If you want to stop sharing connected vehicle data with Ford, the company says to find Vehicle Connectivity in your vehicle's settings and turn it off. However, this broader change can limit connected services and other features. Ford provides additional guidance through its official privacy settings page. GM WANTS DRIVERS TO TAKE THEIR EYES OFF THE ROAD BY 2028 Change privacy preferences in the Ford app You can also adjust certain information-sharing preferences through the Ford app on your smartphone. Ford also provides controls related to Google Maps in the app and certain preferred dealer notifications. Keep in mind that the app's personalization and marketing controls are separate from the vehicle's main connectivity controls. Changing one does not necessarily change the other. If you own more than one Ford, review each vehicle's settings separately. Review what Ford already knows about you You may also want to find out what personal information Ford already holds. The company provides options to request access to personal data and seek corrections or deletion, subject to applicable privacy laws and exceptions. You can find those options through Ford's privacy notice. If you're selling or trading in your Ford, perform a factory reset to remove stored personal information from the vehicle. Ford says this can erase saved addresses, connected accounts and programmed garage door opener codes. You should also make sure the vehicle is disconnected from your Ford account. Depending on its connectivity equipment, you may need to remove the vehicle's VIN from your account as well. Simply deleting the Ford app will not stop vehicle data sharing. However, that reset will not erase data the company already received. Any request to delete that information must be handled separately. Does Ford's promise mean your data stays completely private? There's an important point worth keeping in mind. Ford's commitment about selling driving behavior data to brokers and insurers is specific. It does not prohibit every form of data collection or disclosure. Ford's privacy notice describes circumstances in which information may be shared with service providers or other parties. It also addresses disclosures made in response to valid legal requests. Meanwhile, Ford offers personalization and marketing settings that deserve a separate review. And even though Ford says it doesn't sell driving behavior data to insurance companies, that doesn't mean an insurer can't collect information about how you drive through a separate smartphone app or a voluntary insurance monitoring program. There are also exceptions to Ford's privacy controls. The company says it may collect vehicle location data in certain circumstances even when location sharing is turned off. These can include legal requirements, emergencies and protection of property. Vehicles equipped with the Ford Security Package may also share location information when a Theft Alert is triggered. So even with Ford's new promise, I would still encourage drivers to examine their individual settings. A company can make a meaningful privacy commitment while continuing to collect information needed for its services. And if you're shopping for a new vehicle, consider privacy before making the purchase. What this means to you If you own a newer Ford, this announcement gives you a good reason to check your privacy settings. You may discover that your vehicle shares more information than you expected. You might also find settings you can disable without affecting the features you enjoy. However, you should understand the tradeoff before switching off all connectivity. Losing remote access or other useful services could be inconvenient, especially if you rely on them regularly. The same advice applies if you drive another brand. Take a few minutes to find your manufacturer's privacy settings and learn what information your vehicle shares. You can explore the broader privacy concerns in our article, What your car knows about you and could be telling the world. Ultimately, knowing what your car collects gives you a better chance of controlling your personal information. DATA BROKERS DON'T JUST COLLECT FACTS. THEY GUESS ABOUT YOU Kurt's key takeaways I like seeing Ford make a public commitment about protecting driving data. Especially after what we've learned about how vehicle information can end up in the hands of insurance companies. But here's what I keep coming back to. When you spend tens of thousands of dollars on a vehicle, how much of your personal information should you have to share to enjoy the features you already paid for? I understand why Ford needs certain data to make connected technology work. Real-time traffic updates can be useful. So can getting an alert before a mechanical problem leaves you stranded. But I also think automakers need to make privacy choices much easier to understand. Drivers shouldn't have to dig through complicated menus to figure out what's happening with their information. Ford's promise is encouraging, and I hope other manufacturers pay attention. The real test will be how well these commitments hold up as vehicles become even more connected. Would you sacrifice features like remote start or live navigation to keep your driving data private, or should automakers be required to offer those conveniences without collecting so much personal information? articles.title: America ‘will have a heart attack’: Ray Dalio issues fresh warning on US economy — with savers at highest risk
articles.summary: But it doesn’t end there: “You are at risk,” according to Dalio.
articles.body:
Moneywise and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue through links in the content below.

Ray Dalio sounded like a doctor delivering bad news. The damage had been building for years, and by the time he described what could happen next, he was using two words nobody wants to hear.

"We are very exposed to a heart attack," he said (1) in a recent interview with "Money Rehab."

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 5 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Gold has overtaken U.S. Treasuries as central banks' top reserve asset. Get Goldco's 2026 Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free

But the patient he had in mind wasn't just one person. It was the entirety of America.

The billionaire founder of Bridgewater Associates compared the financial system to the body's circulatory system. And he had a grim way of describing what happens when you let the debt pile up.

"It's like plaque," he said. Over time, the payments squeeze out money that could have gone toward everything else.

"I would say you've accumulated a lot of plaque and you are at risk," Dalio said.

Then he put a number on what it would take to avert a crisis.

"If we don't cut the budget deficit down to 3% of GDP — it's now probably going to be about six and a half percent of GDP — if we don't cut it there, we will have a heart attack," he said.

The government is running a shortfall more than twice Dalio's target. The federal deficit hit $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30, up $217 billion from the year before. That was 6.2% of GDP, according to the Congressional Budget Office (2). By the end of that fiscal year, the total federal debt had reached $40.2 trillion. By Nov. 13, it had crept up to $40.5 trillion (3).

As Dalio pointed out, Washington is already spending more on interest than the Pentagon spends on its military activities. The CBO put net interest on the public debt at $1.14 trillion for the year, compared with $917 billion in military spending by the Department of Defense.

Those may sound like numbers for Washington to worry about. But Dalio warns that how the government deals with its debt could determine how much your savings can buy.

"Either interest rates have to go up and constrict the demand … or the Federal Reserve has to come in and print money and buy all this debt, which is inflationary. In either case, it has the effect of reducing buying power," he said.

articles.summary: U.S. air traffic is slowly returning to normal after a nationwide ground stop Friday halted flights and left thousands canceled and delayed. articles.body:
U.S. air traffic is slowly returning to normal after a nationwide ground stop Friday halted flights and left thousands canceled and delayed.

As of Saturday morning, nearly 2,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. are delayed, and nearly 3,800 have been canceled, according to flight tracking website FlightAware.

FlightAware shows Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, the busiest in the world, with the most delays — 54 — and the most cancellations — 85, followed by Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport and New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport.

Flights were grounded for hours on Friday, a rare move that has been used in only extraordinary circumstances — a human-error outage in 2023, and on Sept. 11, 2001, after the terror attacks. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) cited a telecommunications outage as the cause for the ground stop.

Even once the ground stop was lifted, delays and cancellations began to pile up and create a backlog that may take days to get back on track. Airlines began responding to the disruptions, offering waivers and special assistance to affected passengers.

United , Delta and Southwest all said they would waive all fare differences and change fees to allow passengers to change flights.

“Thank you for your patience as we work to restore our full schedule,” United Airlines wrote on the social platform X. “There are no fees to change your flight, and we’ll waive any fare difference.”

American Airlines waived change fees and is offering refunds, but still requires passengers to pay a fare difference.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that operations are “slowly returning to normal” Saturday morning, but that delays and cancellations will persist as adjustments are made to get air travel back on track.

“You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most,” Duffy wrote on X.
