The nationwide grounding began at around 4 p.m. EST and lasted several hours impacting travel plans for multiple teams including Ole Miss, Kansas State University, University of Utah…
articles.body:
Friday’s nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has led to some changes in Saturday’s schedule for several college football games across the country.

The nationwide grounding began at around 4 p.m. EST and lasted several hours impacting travel plans for multiple teams including Ole Miss, Kansas State University, University of Utah and Arizona State University and University of Minnesota among others.

In the NCAA’s Big 12 Conference, games including Arizona State-UCF and Kansas-West Virginia were delayed by two hours from 3:30 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. EST on Saturday, USA Today reported . The Utah-Arizona kickoff was pushed to 10:30 p.m. EST, with the Utah team flying to Tucson Saturday morning.

In the Big Ten, Michigan State vs Washington has been moved back slightly to 5:30 p.m. It was originally scheduled for 4:15 p.m., the report said.

The Southeastern Conference’s Auburn-Mississippi State matchup was pushed back four hours from noon to 4:15 p.m., while Ole Miss-Oklahoma has been moved to Sunday at 1 p.m. EST, the conference updated in separate posts on social platform X.

The Ole Miss team was not able to depart on Friday due to the nationwide ground stop, and a late-night flight could not be accommodated, according to the statement. The team’s departure has been delayed until Saturday afternoon. The game was originally scheduled for 4:15 p.m. Saturday.

The FAA lifted the stop at around 8:15 p.m. , Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed during a White House press briefing Friday night. He noted that the return to normal flight operations is expected to be “slow.”

“It’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon,” Duffy said.

Duffy attributed the incident to an overload of data on routers, with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin adding the “public was never in danger in this process.”

articles.title: Musk: ‘Critical deals will be lost’ at Nvidia without Huang

articles.body:
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on Saturday that Nvidia will lose “critical deals” after CEO Jensen Huang’s exit from the company following reports of his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Musk wrote in a post on social platform X . “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

Huang’s resignation was announced Thursday following scrutiny over accusations stemming from a New York Times report in October that claimed American authorities discovered Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang illegally smuggled AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with the now-former Nvidia chief.

The resignation came a day after the Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a separate affair with a Nvidia executive who reported to him, citing five people who worked at the company.

Musk has previously hinted his support for the former Nvidia CEO, saying it “would be an honor” to hire him, prior to his resignation, in response to a post on X.

President Trump, in a Truth Social post, suggested that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should be the one to take Jensen Huang’s place, saying, “there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple.”

“A Legend replaces a Legend!” the president wrote in his post.

Following the initial Times report, Nvidia’s board had announced Sunday that it would initiate an independent investigation into the matter. On Tuesday, the company said it hired former acting U.S. Attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to conduct the investigation.

Huang admitted in a statement that he has been unfaithful to his wife, adding, “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” according to a report from Bloomberg .

He was called by GOP lawmakers to appear in a joint, closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 to address concerns regarding Nvidia’s security protocols and his interactions with the alleged spy.

articles.title: Pennsylvania, Wisconsin report additional deaths linked to measles
articles.summary: The U.S. reached 10 measles deaths this year after additional deaths reported in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, a concerning sign as the previously eradicated disease makes a resurgence worldwide and in the U.S. Measles cases have already reached more than 5,400 this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) dashboard — more…
articles.body:
The U.S. reached 10 measles deaths this year after additional deaths reported in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, a concerning sign as the previously eradicated disease makes a resurgence worldwide and in the U.S.

Measles cases have already reached more than 5,400 this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) dashboard — more than double the nearly 2,300 reported through the entirety of 2025.

Ninety-six percent of cases in 2026 are in unvaccinated individuals, compared to 93 percent last year.

Pennsylvania’s department of health confirmed that the newly added measles death, which brings the total to 7 deaths in the commonwealth, was in an unvaccinated person. Wisconsin said that a child had died but did not specify other details .

The Keystone State, with more than 1,500 cases, accounts for more than 1 in 4 cases reported in the entire country, according to the state’s dashboard .

Despite previously being eradicated in the U.S., measles has made a resurgence as vaccination rates have declined.

Pennsylvania issued a warning to doctors last month that the commonwealth had identified a case of congenital measles — measles transmitted from a mother to her newborn — for the first time in decades.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) were locked in a bitter dispute earlier this year after Shapiro said Kennedy, a longtime vaccine skeptic, was “spreading misinformation.” Kennedy said there was no evidence of that.

President Trump signed an executive order earlier this year recommending splitting the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate shots, claiming without evidence that it is “quite lethal.”

The CDC sent a “disease detective” to Pennsylvania in October to assist the state in responding to the outbreak.

articles.body:
An internet trade group, representing 30 members including Google, YouTube, Facebook and Instagram, has sued the state of New York challenging its law that requires social media platforms ​to provide state-approved warning labels ‌for users.

NetChoice’s complaint said the state law violates the free-speech protections or First Amendment rights, Reuters reported .

The law, that was signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul (D-N.Y.) last year, requires social media platforms to warn about potential harm to younger users, the report said. It is scheduled to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

“Unlike a static warning on ​a product label, these warnings repeatedly interrupt users and ​block access ⁠to protected speech,” NetChoice noted.

Earlier this month , similar lawsuits were filed by Meta, TikTok and Google against California which argued that the state’s bipartisan “ Digital Age Assurance Act ,” violated both the First Amendment and the federal Communications Decency Act.

The Communications Decency Act protects online platforms from being sued over third party content. California’s Digital Age Assurance Act was also set to go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

The California law would ban social media platforms from providing “an addictive feed” to users under the age of 16. It would also require social media companies to “implement reasonable measures” to prevent minors from accessing such features.

The legal battles over children’s safety and social media have been brewing in recent months.

Last month, West Virginia sued TikTok and its parent company, ByteDance, alleging that the social media company violated state consumer protection laws by using addictive features to encourage excessive screen time among children.

The state also accused the platform of overstating the effectiveness of its parental controls while failing to address gaps that could allow predators to contact children.

In August, California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey faced Meta in a high-profile trial , as part of a coalition of 29 states suing the company for allegedly designing features to keep minors hooked on social media and deceiving parents about the safety of the platforms. Later that month, a $17 billion settlement was reached in the case.

Separately, Meta would have to pay Texas more than $1 billion over similar allegations , bringing the tech giant’s total payment sum to just more than $18 billion.

articles.title: Work to replace old copper wire led to the FAA’s ground stop
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says that issues with a new router related to a fiber optic upgrade grounded thousands of flights on Friday.
articles.body: At a press conference today, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that Friday’s nationwide ground stop ordered by the FAA was related to work replacing outdated copper wire with a fiber optic line at a “remote FAA facility.” The secretary said that this was “routine maintenance,” rather than the result of a major modernization effort. He told reporters that it was “such an old wire that it was being discontinued, meaning that line was going to get shut down,” necessitating the upgrade. What wasn’t clear, according to Secretary Duffy, was the root cause of the problem. He said that it could have been faulty hardware, a misconfigured router, or “incompetence” on the part of contractor L3Harris. Regardless, what followed was the newly installed router “flooding” other routers in the Air Traffic Control system. Duffy said that there were “over 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” causing disruption to radar feeds and communication with planes. [Media: Secretary Duffy also took the opportunity to call on additional funding from Congress for modernizing the Air Traffic Control system, and to tout the work the FAA has done so far. “We are building, we are building safely, but we are building fast,” he said, but said that Congress had only given him a “partial payment” to complete the necessary work. In a statement posted to their site, L3Harris said: > L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously. Update November 14th: Added a statement from L3Harris.

articles.title: Transportation secretary blames ‘routine’ equipment upgrade for grounding flights nationwide | TechCrunch
articles.summary: FAA administrator Bryan Bedford also said there's "zero evidence of anything AI-related."
articles.body:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that a nationwide ground stop halting flights across the United States was caused by seemingly routine maintenance work.

Duffy said that during “routine maintenance,” copper wire at a remote location was being upgraded to fiber optic cable by L3Harris, a longtime contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration. After the upgrade, a router overloaded a critical communication system, leading to the ground stop.

“It’s pretty straightforward work that we were doing yesterday at, again, a very remote location,” Duffy said during a Saturday press conference that appeared to have technical issues of its own . “What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence — meaning, was it user error or installator error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?”

The FAA’s acting CTO Rebecca Guy added , “When we started to see the occurrence where our network was having instability, we started to look at what was the cause. And as such, we saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate — a thousand connections over every four to five seconds.”

Guy said the FAA disabled “both of those, right away and were able to stabilize our network,” and is now performing a root cause analysis.

Duffy has repeatedly insisted, at multiple press conferences, that Congress needs to provide more funding for aviation equipment upgrades. Asked why the upgrades were made at 3pm on a Friday afternoon — rather than, say, at midnight on a Saturday — he responded that while “switchovers” at bigger airports will take place late at night, remote switchovers happen during the day.

“There will be reevaluation of when we do this work,” he said.

This was only the third nationwide ground stop of the 21st century. More than 8,200 flights were canceled on Friday evening, according to aviation data firm Cirium . And the effects continued after the ground stop was lifted, with at least another 3,000 flights canceled on Saturday.

The ground stop came just a day after the FAA announced the rollout of an AI tool for air traffic controllers; the air traffic controllers union said it was not consulted in designing the system. However, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency sees “zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI-related.”

“We want to be clear that we have an equipment issue, and we’re working through what this defective piece of equipment was,” Bedford said.

When Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was asked earlier if the ground stop was caused by AI, he replied , “We call it SI around here, remember? SI.”

articles.title: 5 things to know on the FAA groundings
articles.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has air traffic control systems back online after a major telecommunications outage grounded all U.S. flights Friday evening. The delay stranded passengers across the country and forced airlines to delay or cancel thousands of flights, a disruption that may take days to get back to normal. Those affected included everyday…
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has air traffic control systems back online after a major telecommunications outage grounded all U.S. flights Friday evening.

The delay stranded passengers across the country and forced airlines to delay or cancel thousands of flights, a disruption that may take days to get back to normal. Those affected included everyday passengers, but also college football teams traveling to big matchups for Saturday.

Government officials have initially identified old equipment as the reason for the failure and have requested additional funding to modernize air traffic control systems.

Here are five things to know about the nationwide ground stop.

Nearly 4,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. were delayed as of late Saturday morning, and more than 4,300 have been canceled, according to flight tracking website FlightAware.

Those delays and cancellations have only increased throughout the morning, and are concentrated at the busiest airports. Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport, Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport and New York’s John F. Kennedy (JFK) International Airport remain the three with the most disruptions.

Fifteen percent of all flights in Atlanta, the world’s busiest airport, have been canceled, with another nearly 20 percent delayed. Twenty percent of flights out of JFK have been canceled.

Airlines have begun accommodating passengers whose flights were disrupted. All four of the major airlines — Delta, United, Southwest and American — are waiving change fees for affected passengers, and Delta, United and Southwest are waiving fare differences to allow customers to change their flights at no additional cost.

Old communications systems seen as culprit

At a press conference Saturday, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that a wire switch may have caused the telecommunications outage.

Duffy said a contractor called L3Harris was replacing an old copper wire with a new fiber cable, and that the FAA was investigating to see if that was the cause.

“So what we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router?” Duffy said. “We haven’t determined what the fault was.”

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency has not identified any evidence of malice, such as a cyberattack.

“We see zero evidence of anything nefarious. It is an equipment issue,” Bedford told reporters. “When we have this root-cause analysis complete we will share it with you.”

College football teams race to make games

The travel disruptions hit right as college football teams were preparing to take off for anticipated Saturday matchups.

Games in the Big 12, Big Ten and Southeastern Conference were delayed Saturday, in some cases by several hours, due to the disruptions. The Ole Miss-Oklahoma game was moved to Sunday afternoon.

In the NFL, the league updated its officiating assignments to keep officials within driving distance of their homes amid the flight disruptions.

Trump officials plead for congressional dollars

At a joint press conference Friday night with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Duffy asked Congress to pass more than $50 billion in funding for modernizing air traffic control systems in the U.S.

“I want $50 billion,” Duffy told reporters. “Let’s finish this job: new hardware, new software, new telecommunication.”

Duffy has made a big push to modernize the FAA and air traffic control systems in his role as transportation secretary, pointing to decades-old systems that rely on old technology. Mullin echoed Duffy’s claims, calling for a “complete overhaul of the system.”

The transportation secretary shared his message to members of Congress.

“Give President Trump — give Duffy the money. Let them finish this job so we don’t have to do a press conference at 8:30 at night ever again,’” Duffy said.

As federal officials say they are investigating the cause of Friday’s incident, a key House Democrat is raising questions .

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the likely next chair of the House Oversight Committee, called the ground stop “quite disturbing” in an interview on MS NOW Friday.

“Whatever it is, I think deserves as much transparency as possible,” Garcia said.

The California Democrat has already pledged to investigate the president and his allies, which the White House vowed to aggressively respond to.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), the likely candidate for Speaker of the House, released a statement accusing the administration of “failed leadership.”

“American travelers deserve timely answers from the Trump Administration about how and why this happened and assurances that steps are being taken to ensure that our air travel system remains safe and functional,” Jeffries said.

articles.title: Johnson says ‘we don’t really need any investigation’ on FAA ground stop
articles.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said there is no need for an investigation into the ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday, instead highlighting the need for “investment.” “We don’t really need any investigation … we need further investment,” Johnson said during an interview with Fox News’s Saturday in America. “I…
articles.body:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said there is no need for an investigation into the ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday, instead highlighting the need for “investment.”

“We don’t really need any investigation … we need further investment,” Johnson said during an interview with Fox News’s Saturday in America . “I mean, some of this equipment dates back to the eighties so it’s gotta be updated and that’s our responsibility. We’re gonna work to get it done.”

The FAA issued the nationwide ground stop around 4 p.m. EST on Friday. The rare protocol was in place for over four hours. The agency’s last widespread stoppage, which lasted approximately 90 minutes, was in January 2023.

The FAA lifted the stop at around 8:15 p.m. , Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed during a White House press briefing Friday night.

Duffy attributed the incident to an overload of data on routers, with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin adding the “public was never in danger in this process.”

During the briefing, the officials called for a multi-billion-dollar investment into updating the U.S.’s “incredibly old” air traffic control systems.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said during the Friday night briefing. “Let’s not do a patchwork, a fix to a system that’s critical for every single family.”

Duffy in September asked Congress for $30 billion to fund new technology, control towers and airport improvements across the country.

In a press briefing Saturday morning, Duffy said a telecommunications line switch by a contractor may have started Friday’s FAA ground stoppage. He noted that an older copper wire was being replaced by a new fiber cable by contractor L3Harris.

More than 4,500 flights within, into or out of the U.S. were delayed as of Saturday afternoon with over 5,000 canceled, according to flight tracking website FlightAware. Total reported delays on Saturday crossed 15,000.

articles.title: Italy fines Meta $887M for accessing users’ photos without specific consent
articles.summary: Italy announced Saturday it is handing Meta an $887 million fine for using photos and videos from Android users’ Facebook galleries without specific consent. Investigators found Facebook had enabled a “get suggestions from gallery when browsing” feature by default and requested access to users’ personal photo library through a single permission notice, according to a…
articles.body:
Italy announced Saturday it is handing Meta an $887 million fine for using photos and videos from Android users’ Facebook galleries without specific consent.

Investigators found Facebook had enabled a “get suggestions from gallery when browsing” feature by default and requested access to users’ personal photo library through a single permission notice, according to a release from the Italian Data Protection Authority naming Meta’s Irish subsidiary.

The agency said the “generic” nature of the authorization notice violated an Italian law that protects smartphones as part of a person’s private sphere and requires “free and informed consent” for access. The law stems from the European Union’s broader “ePrivacy Directive.”

It gave Meta 60 days to make the feature “turned off by default” and adjust the consent notice to include “a separate and specific request for the feature and clearly explain to users what it is for, that it involves access to the gallery, and how to disable it.”

The fine comes as Meta faces multiple legal battles in the U.S. regarding children’s use of its social media platforms, many alleging its sites are unsafe for young users due to addictive qualities.

In August, California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey faced Meta in a high-profile trial as part of a coalition of 29 states suing the company for allegedly designing features to keep minors hooked on social media and deceiving parents about the safety of the platforms. Later that month, the states reached a $17 billion settlement with the tech giant.

That same month, Meta separately awarded Texas an over $1 billion payout over similar allegations , bringing the tech giant’s total payment sum to around $18 billion.

Following the “blue wave” that swept the nation on Nov. 3, with Democrats securing stunning victories in the midterms, AI safety advocates are hopeful the new Congress will support stricter tech industry regulation.

With several incoming lawmakers having a record of supporting AI guardrails, such as Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) as well as Rep.-elects Manny Rutinel (Colo.), Micah Lasher (N.Y.) and others, the emerging technology will likely come under the microscope of both Democrat-run chambers.

The Hill has reached out to Meta for comment on Italy’s fine.

articles.title: Microsoft services fully restored after global disruptions
articles.summary: Microsoft confirmed its services are fully restored as of Saturday after the tech company faced a massive global outage impacting its platforms earlier in the week. “We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” the company wrote in a post…
articles.body:
Microsoft confirmed its services are fully restored as of Saturday after the tech company faced a massive global outage impacting its platforms earlier in the week.

“We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” the company wrote in a post to social platform X just after midnight using its “Microsoft 365 Status” account, which provides official updates on service incidents.

A day after Thursday’s widespread outage, Microsoft said it was “ seeing encouraging recovery progress ” but added users may “experience intermittent issues.” It also noted at the time the incident was the result of a “technical issue” as opposed to a cyberattack or the interference of a rogue AI agents — both of which have made headlines in recent months.

The outage started at around 11:17 a.m. EST Thursday, impacting hallmark Microsoft platforms such as Outlook and Teams. The tech firm said the incident was “introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change.”

According to data from Downdetector, an online service issues tracker, the outage hit 74 countries within one hour. The incident caused interruptions across industries — including healthcare, banking and the government, among others, The Associated Press reported .

The United Kingdom’s National Pharmacy Association said in a statement Friday Microsoft email disruptions were affecting pharmacies’ ability to communicate with doctors.

In countries like Singapore, Japan, Greece and Norway, the outage impacted government operations, including email communications for certain ministries or agencies, according to the AP.

“We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions,” Microsoft said in a separate Friday statement .

“Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration,” it added.

articles.title: Federalist Society’s celebrations mix with shock over Democratic sweep
articles.summary: Two years ago, a champagne cork went flying on the Federalist Society convention stage as panelists toasted recent Supreme Court wins. A celebratory mood was still on display at this year’s annual gathering of the conservative legal movement, but those feelings were mixed with shock from Democrats’ midterm victories. “On election night, there was a congressman…
articles.body:
Two years ago, a champagne cork went flying on the Federalist Society convention stage as panelists toasted recent Supreme Court wins. A celebratory mood was still on display at this year’s annual gathering of the conservative legal movement, but those feelings were mixed with shock from Democrats’ midterm victories.

“On election night, there was a congressman who said we all need to lawyer up. So, here we are,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio joked to attendees Friday evening.

The Federalist Society has become a tentpole of the conservative legal movement in the course of its 40-year history.

Law students founded the group in the 1980s, seeking to combat liberal ideology on college campuses, but it has since developed into a pipeline for aspiring conservative lawyers as they journey from law schools to prominent firms — and in some cases, administration positions or judgeships.

The Supreme Court’s 6-3 conservative supermajority emerged as the crown jewel of that project.

Leonard Leo, the Federalist Society’s longtime leader who extended its influence in part by building an extensive network of major donors, created the lists President Trump used to select his high court nominees during his first term: Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett.

Now back in the White House for his second term, Trump has publicly sparred with the Federalist Society after some of the president’s own judicial nominees struck down his signature agenda items. Last year, Trump took to calling Leo a “sleazebag.”

That fray had already raised questions about the future of the president’s judicial selections. Now that Democrats are retaking the Senate — with some pundits predicting the party could maintain control in future cycles — discourse around whether Trump will be able to build on his legacy of appointing conservative judges has grown. And Republican senators are racing to confirm remaining vacancies before the change of power in January.

Democrats’ sweeping victories in traditionally red states like Mississippi and Kansas left some lawyers dazed as they traveled to the nation’s capital for this week’s convention.

“Did you think it would be this bad?” one lawyer at a prominent conservative legal group asked after learning the person he had sat next to for lunch was from Texas.

In addition to flipping Texas’s open Senate and gubernatorial posts, Democrats claimed multiple seats on its supreme court for the first time in years as well as in its attorney general’s office.

Mariah Cermone, president emerita of the Federalist Society’s Texas student chapter, noted the Lone Star State’s new dynamic as she introduced one its Republican justices to deliver the convention’s opening address.

“Even though Texans have taken to troubleshooting their grievances by holding their breath till they happen to turn blue, I must say that I still choose Texas every day of the week and twice on Sunday,” said Cermone, a native Floridian.

Another conservative law professor, John Yoo — who currently works at University of California at Berkley but is set to move next year to the University of Texas — joked, “I can’t even find a red state to move to.” He called the midterm results “stunning” while speaking on a panel.

“I think the American people supported President Trump’s effort to restore order at the border, but gosh, I think that the challenge to birthright citizenship was a serious mistake,” Yoo said. “Overaggressive enforcement of immigration laws that resulted in the killing of two American citizens was a serious mistake.”

Still, the convention was full of celebration, both over America’s 250th birthday — which it honored with a themed bar and merchandise — and the conservative movement’s continued victories before the Supreme Court.

Rubio, who delivered the conference’s Barbara K. Olson Memorial Lecture on Friday, encouraged attendees not to be dismayed by the political setbacks.

“Great things that last are built in decades, not election cycles,” Rubio, a leading contender for the Republican presidential nomination in 2028, said.

One law student framed the election outcome as merely part of a historical norm, saying he didn’t see the “purpose” of being negative about the movement’s long-term prospects.

“This is not the end of our country that we had, you know, one bad midterm performance,” Will Schwieterman, who attends the University of Chicago, said in an interview. “It’s only the end if we stop fighting for what we believe in, stop standing for the Constitution, and you know, just kind of accept things as how they are.”

That optimistic tone was on display throughout the convention.

After Alliance for Consumers Executive Director O.H. Skinner moderated a session, he gifted attendees commemorative coins to “lift your spirits about the future of the law in our nation.”

The coins celebrated the conservative legal movement’s “generational wins” at the Supreme Court last term. Each coin lists one of four decisions: expanding presidential firing power, narrowing the Voting Rights Act, allowing states to enforce transgender athlete bans and invalidating Hawaii’s gun restrictions.

“The recently completed Supreme Court term demonstrated the Court’s continued commitment to building and expanding off past generational wins and its ability to continue successfully tackling new and emerging questions of great societal importance,” Skinner wrote in an accompanying note.

As Trump’s Supreme Court appointees all participated in a video for the convention, Justice Samuel Alito delivered the keynote at the annual dinner.

Though Alito didn’t directly reference the midterms, he warned Congress could make good on its past threats to use the power of the purse.

Some Democrats and outside groups have previously floated taking a congressional vote to defund the court’s operations — seeking to put pressure on the conservative justices to change course.

“Congress can turn off the lights at the Supreme Court and stop everything from happening if they want to defund their activities. And there are many, many, many other things that they can do, or at least try to do,” Alito warned.

Reflecting on his two decades on the court, Alito celebrated recent decisions on abortion, religious rights and other major issues. The justice reflected on these rulings, saying much progress had been made to “try to back toward the original structure” of the Constitution.

“How that is going to play out in the future, and how far it should play out in the future, and whether — those are open questions,” Alito said.

“But those are all very important questions,” the justice said in his final words of the evening.

images.caption: United States Supreme Court Justice Amy Coney Barrett, center, was the main speaker at the 2023 Antonin Scalia Memorial Dinner that was part of the Federalist Society’s 2023 National Lawyers Convention at the Washington Hilton Hotel on Nov. 9, 2023, in Washington. Justices Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch, and Samuel Alito were also in attendance.

articles.title: Bigger and more-frequent wildfires threaten water supplies across the US
articles.summary: Wildfires leave behind charred trees and scorched vegetation that impact the streams and rivers providing drinking water to much of the country, and new studies show that contamination could remain for more than a decade.
articles.body:
Wildfires leave behind charred trees and scorched vegetation that impact the streams and rivers providing drinking water to much of the country, and new studies show that contamination could remain for more than a decade.

These findings about the longevity of contamination in the nation’s drinking water supplies are especially concerning as climate change and increasingly strong El Niño weather events, which intensify drought conditions , have led to bigger and more frequent wildfires in the U.S. So far in 2026, there have been 68,179 blazes burning more than 14,062 square miles.

After a wildfire sweeps through hillsides and forests, rains carry ash and organic matter into the streams that feed water treatment plants for towns and cities alike. Communities are working to adapt, but it can take years and require stopgap solutions.

People in the City of Las Vegas, New Mexico , went without water for months after the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon wildfire contaminated the Gallinas River in 2022. In the four years since, they’ve had to give residents bottled water and ship tanks in from nearby towns as they collected funds to build a new treatment plant.

Karen Pettine, who has owned the Hillcrest Restaurant for 50 years, said the water crisis forced them to close, sometimes for a week at a time.

“It’s hard to run a restaurant without good water,” she said. “We used some paper plates at times. They brought in semi-truckloads of bottled water. You could pick up four cases at a time. The water situation is ongoing because when it rains, it floods and it brings dirty water down the stream.”

Las Vegas Mayor David Romero said climate change has made the things that used to be reliable less predictable.

“It’s a scary situation that we’re all going to encounter,” he said.

Sediment from burned landscapes a headache for water-treatment plants

Wildfires are a natural part of forest ecosystems, but an increase in their severity has made areas that capture, filter and regulate the flow of water, known as watersheds, vulnerable, said Amanda Hohner, an assistant professor at Montana State University who specializes in wildfires and water quality.

Forested watersheds provide water to nearly two-thirds of municipalities in the U.S., according to Carli Brucker, lead author of a University of Colorado Boulder study that assessed wildfire-affected water quality in hundreds of burned basins and compared them to unburned areas. Their study found that the impacts can last up to eight years.

Garrett McKay, an associate professor of civil and environmental engineering at Texas A&M, said utilities are extremely concerned about the impacts wildfires have on water. They’re reaching out to experts like him for help finding different water sources or to learn how to treat the organic matter coming into their plants.

Water treatment facilities that rely on streams and rivers typically treat high quality water, aided by trees and soil that act as a natural filtration system, Brucker said. But wildfires cause spikes in heavy metals or dissolved organic matter, which the plants aren’t built to handle, she said.

This can force treatment facilities to shut off the incoming water and resort to other sources, which may not be immediately available, Brucker said. Some have groundwater or reservoir backups, but even those can be impacted.

Reservoirs can serve as a “sedimentation basin” where particles can settle, said Kyle Shimabuku, an associate professor of civil engineering at Gonzaga University. But sediments from burned vegetation are rich in nutrients, like nitrogen and phosphorus, and as they sit in still water, algal blooms can grow, he said. The algae can make people sick and kill the fish.

Chlorine, routinely used to treat water, also is impacted by wildfires, said McKay at Texas A&M. When facilities add disinfectants, like chlorine, to water, they react with the dissolved organic matter left behind by the fires to form “disinfection byproducts,” which are regulated by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency because they can cause illnesses, including cancer.

Since plants can’t remove the disinfection byproducts, they must get rid of the organic matter before disinfecting the water, which can cause delays in the water supply.

Implementing new options can cost facilities millions

When a 2020 wildfire burned the area around No Name and Grizzly creeks, the primary water sources for the city of Glenwood Springs, Colorado, officials scrambled to protect against sediment expected to wash down the slopes when spring rains arrived. They sought help from the Colorado Water Conservation Board. Within two months, the board authorized an emergency loan of $8 million for improvements to the treatment system.

Fort Collins faced a similar challenge that year when ash and sediment from the Cameron Peak fire forced the city to close its river intake and pull water from the Horsetooth Reservoir, which was safe to use because it’s fed by a different watershed.

Las Vegas, New Mexico, was hit harder when the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon fire damaged the Gallinas River watershed in 2022. A massive rainstorm swept ash and sludge from the burn scar into the river and reservoirs, forcing the town to shut down its water treatment plant while they installed additional filters and looked for additional water sources.

As they worked on solutions, a massive flood in 2024 carried more burn debris into the town’s two reservoirs, leaving them with only a few days of safe water. As businesses closed and residents bought bottled water, the town hired trucks to bring 2.2 million gallons (8.3 million liters) of water from nearby towns of Santa Fe and Santa Rosa.

They were hit again in February 2025. Burn scar debris coupled with bad weather and equipment failure caused a pressure drop, which resulted in a monthlong boil-water advisory and more water shipments.

“The February event was probably the scariest,” Romero said.

Ultimately, the state and federal governments allocated $148 million to rebuild the town’s treatment plant and help support their efforts to find other options, including drilling wells and reusing water. Groundbreaking on the first phase of their new water treatment plant is slated for Nov. 18, the mayor said.

“We’ve been doing a lot of work for other sources of water and we know with climate change and what we experienced in the past, the Gallinas River is something we can’t depend on forever.”

articles.title: SpaceX catches Starship for first time, drawing praise in Washington
articles.summary: SpaceX’s Starship aircraft successfully touched back down at a South Texas launch site Saturday afternoon — marking a historic milestone in the aerospace giant’s effort to build reusable rockets. The 170-foot-long spacecraft launched from Starbase, Texas, on Friday for its 15th flight, the Elon Musk-headed company wrote in a Saturday release. Once it got into orbit,…
articles.body:
SpaceX’s Starship aircraft successfully touched back down at a South Texas launch site Saturday afternoon — marking a historic milestone in the aerospace giant’s effort to build reusable rockets.

The 170-foot-long spacecraft launched from Starbase, Texas, on Friday for its 15th flight, the Elon Musk-headed company wrote in a Saturday release. Once it got into orbit, Starship deployed 26 of the company’s Starlink V3 satellites before returning to Earth, where it was caught for the first time in its launch tower, dubbed “Mechzilla.”

Previously, SpaceX had successfully landed a portion of its smaller Falcon 9 rocket, but the upper stages of these launch models were discarded before reentering the Earth’s atmosphere.

The successful landing marks the company’s first return of a Starship from orbit in a debut attempt at this feat.

The company had aimed to also catch the bottom half of the rocket, in what is called a “double catch” maneuver, but the booster was diverted to a splashdown because of a detected guidance problem, according to SpaceX.

Musk noted in a social media post that, while there was a “slight underperformance of engines” in Saturday’s attempt, the landing still marks a significant victory for the future of space travel.

“These early ships and boosters are already outdated by improved designs in production or on the test stand, so this booster loss does not change our timeline to reach high volume, fully reusable Starship flights,” he added.

Members and allies of the Trump administration celebrated the achievement in a barrage of social media posts Saturday.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman called the feat “almost magic” in a post to social platform X.

Brendan Carr, the chair of the Federal Exchange Commission, called the landing “amazing” in a separate post and congratulated Musk and the SpaceX team. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth similarly celebrated the tech mogul for being “a great American.”

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle also commented on the landing, lauding the catch as a significant achievement.

Democratic Rep. Ted Lieu (Calif.) wrote in a post responding to a video of the successful recapture, “Congratulations to SpaceX for making history with an amazing feat of engineering!”

Pennsylvania Sen. Dave McCormick (R) also commended Musk and his rocket company.

“A vivid reminder that despite all our challenges, we live in the land of freedom and innovation, the best place in the world to dream impossible dreams,” he wrote. “We need to preserve and expand that culture of possibility, risk-taking, and creativity for all our citizens.”

articles.title: Crypto was hoping for a breakthrough in Congress. Now it’s bracing for investigations
articles.summary: The cryptocurrency industry is bracing for a changing of the guard in Congress, as Democrats take control of both the House and Senate with a more skeptical eye toward digital assets. After a major crypto regulation bill came up short in the Senate in September, the industry sees limited prospects for the legislation in either…
articles.body:
The cryptocurrency industry is bracing for a changing of the guard in Congress, as Democrats take control of both the House and Senate with a more skeptical eye toward digital assets.

After a major crypto regulation bill came up short in the Senate in September, the industry sees limited prospects for the legislation in either the jam-packed lame-duck session or the new Congress.

Instead, the crypto world is preparing for a whirlwind of investigations from newly Democratic-controlled committees, while keeping up hope for smaller policy wins over the next two years.

“There’s not a ton of positive here” for the industry, said Chris Niebuhr, a senior research analyst at Beacon Policy Advisors.

“The expectation with Sen. [Elizabeth] Warren likely to ascend to the gavel at the Senate Banking Committee and Rep. [Maxine] Waters the leader to take over House Financial Services is that you’ll have more crypto skeptics in positions of power,” he continued.

The crypto industry came into Washington two years ago, riding high on a series of victories. After a years-long battle with Biden-era regulators, it had secured the support of the incoming president and was eyeing favorable prospects for legislation in a GOP-controlled Congress.

Under the Trump administration , the industry quickly saw a shift in the approach to crypto policy. President Trump tapped several crypto-friendly candidates to serve in key roles, while the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) dropped numerous investigations and lawsuits into digital asset firms.

The passage of the GENIUS Act in July 2025 proved to be a high watermark. The measure created a regulatory framework for one form of crypto known as stablecoins, digital tokens tied to stable assets like the U.S. dollar.

But the industry ran headlong into the complicated reality of the Senate when it turned to the Clarity Act , a bill to develop a regulatory structure for the rest of the market and the crown jewel of crypto’s legislative ambitions.

Negotiations between Republicans and crypto-friendly Democrats dragged on for a year amid a series of battles over a stablecoin rewards provision and ethics requirements for federal officials, including the president.

The Clarity Act ultimately came up for a procedural vote on the Senate floor in mid-September and fell short, with every Democrat and a handful of Republicans voting against advancing the measure.

“Frankly, you had a crypto coalition that blew it,” former House Financial Services Chair Patrick McHenry (R-N.C.) told Bloomberg Television in early November.

“They had an opportunity to legislate, and they were holding out for something that was unattainable, a perfect piece of legislation,” he continued. “And rather than take something that was good, many of them held out for perfection, and now have ended up with nothing legislatively.”

While the prospects for the Clarity Act were already looking dim following September’s vote, the results of the midterm elections are adding to the industry’s difficulties.

Democrats secured sweeping victories, including in Ohio, where former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) defeated incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R). It was a particularly bruising loss for the industry, which spent heavily against Brown.

It was a “rough night for crypto,” noted Ian Katz, managing director at Capital Alpha.

The industry spent about $40 million opposing Brown in 2024, when he lost to now-Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). It poured even more into the race this cycle but came up short.

But perhaps most critical to crypto is the prospect of new Democratic leadership on key panels, including the Senate Banking Committee and House Financial Services Committee.

Warren, a fierce crypto critic, is widely expected to take the reins of the Senate Banking panel. Waters is vying for the gavel of the House Financial Services Committee but faces a challenge from Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.).

“The biggest fallout from that is headline risk,” Niebuhr said. “Where you get scrutiny of companies, particularly those with ties in some form or another to the administration.”

Democrats across the board are expected to use their oversight powers in the new Congress. From her perch at Senate Banking, Warren appears likely to take aim at crypto, in addition to Wall Street and other major corporations.

“In the grand scheme of things, that’s maybe a diversion of resources from where those companies want to put them,” Niebuhr added. “But I’m not sure it has a particularly material impact on their overall business.”

The industry’s legislative prospects are also fairly limited. The current Congress has a couple weeks left in session, but there’s little room or incentive to renew the crypto bill.

“It’s off the table for the lame-duck session,” said Brian Gardner, chief Washington policy strategist at the wealth management and investment banking firm Stifel. “I don’t think Democrats at this point are going to go along.”

Looking ahead to the new Congress, he suggested it’s “in the interest of the crypto industry to get legislation passed.”

The SEC and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) have moved forward with their own regulations in the meantime. But it’s unclear how those will stand up over time, particularly under a different administration.

“Legislation, by its very nature, is durable. Maybe not permanent, but durable,” Gardner added. “How that plays out — I have big questions about whether it’s possible.”

Under new leadership, the Clarity Act would likely be changed “in ways that Democrats want and that industry probably doesn’t want,” Katz noted, saying he expects the legislation to move to the “backburner for a while.”

Niebuhr similarly said it’s “hard to see either Democratic majority feel any particularly strong incentive” to revisit the legislation, suggesting that “what happened with Clarity in the Senate kind of poisoned the well.”

A smaller, more bipartisan effort potentially on the table — crypto tax legislation. It has seen some success in this Congress, with the Digital Asset Tax Certainty Act passing out of the House Ways and Means Committee in September.

Kevin Wysocki, head of policy at the crypto firm Anchorage Digital, told The Hill he sees room for tax and potentially national security-related crypto legislation in the new Congress.

“I think market structure is unlikely, but I’m not giving up hope just yet,” he added.

Even as the industry faces an uphill battle on legislation, Katz suggested there is an “opportunity here is to try to show Democrats that they’re not the villains, they’re not the bad guys, and that they too want a safe investor environment.”

Niebuhr also noted the industry might benefit by shifting to a “traditional longer term lobbying presence” focused on relationship building.

“That might be what’s required here, particularly as you have 2028 on the horizon,” he said. “For now, the industry is going to continue to, loosely speaking, get what it wants out of the regulators. And the fear would obviously be that, in 2028, you have a potential for that to no longer be the case.”

articles.title: An overview of Jensen Huang’s messy days
articles.summary: Things moved fast for the now-former CEO of Nvidia.
articles.body: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on Jensen Huang’s resignation and the fallout from Nvidia’s leadership crisis, follow Terrence O’Brien. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started On October 29th, The New York Times reported that Nvidia co-founder and showman CEO Jensen Huang appeared to be the target of a Chinese spy plot. Any major tech CEO potentially being compromised by the Chinese government is concerning — especially Jensen Huang. “If you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that,” Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, previously told The Verge. “If you could draw the diagram of the entire Nvidia ecosystem, a single man is standing at the heart of all of that.” The Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. Alice Huang had been on the American government’s radar for some time, perhaps as early as 2024. Her company was investigated by the US Commerce Department over suspicions it was illegally smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China in violation of US government trade restrictions. Singapore authorities confiscated her passport back in June of 2025, eventually barring her from the country, after she reportedly gave “inaccurate information” to police. And perhaps more concerningly, some US officials believed she was passing information, possibly about Nvidia’s designs or the White House’s deliberations over trade restrictions, directly back to Beijing. This made her relationship with Jensen Huang concerning for multiple reasons. Nvidia’s chips are considered crucial to America’s AI superiority and a matter of national security by the White House. The government has restricted the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China since the Biden administration. But Jensen Huang has routinely pushed to loosen those trade restrictions. Meanwhile, he had gotten quite cozy with President Trump, once even putting him on speakerphone on-stage at the All-In Summit. Then last week, things escalated quickly. On Friday, November 6th, the Times reported that Alice Huang was specifically recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. Though, there is some disagreement among US intelligence officials over the strength of evidence tying Alice Huang to Beijing. While the paper did not confirm it at the time, rumors suggested the “close relationship” between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang was romantic in nature. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair, but did not name the Megaspeed exec and alleged Chinese spy specifically. Nvidia’s board announced that it was launching an investigation into its CEO shortly after. Many believed that Jensen Huang would survive the scandal. His company’s importance to America’s booming AI industry and his crucial role at the company seemed to make him nearly untouchable. He was, after all, the only CEO the company had ever known with no clear and obvious succession plan in place, and he sat atop an unusual corporate structure with around 60 direct reports. (These numbers are slightly outdated, but according to the Harvard Business Review, 10 to 20 is far more common among Fortune 500 companies, and Tim Cook reportedly had 17 in 2015, which was deemed “a lot” by Business Insider.) Then on Wednesday, November 11th, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a second affair — this one with one of his direct reports, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. Whether that was the last straw or if they were afraid it would be merely the tip of the iceberg, the board was ready to push Jensen Huang out, according to reports circulating that evening. According to Bloomberg, he had accepted his fate Wednesday evening reportedly looking “broken and shattered” and telling people, “I’m a piece of shit.” On Thursday, November 12th, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO of Nvidia. How it’s going CFO Colette Kress was immediately named interim CEO, and acknowledged to employees that this has been an “extraordinarily difficult period.” Harvey Jones was also named the first board chair in the company’s history, already signaling there would be some changes to the corporate structure. In a memo to employees, Jones said the company would “search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates.” But the destabilizing impact was immediate. Nvidia’s stock closed at an all-time high of $239.24 on October 6th. It closed at $162.85 on November 13th. It’s hard to overstate the importance of Nvidia to the US’s AI arms race with China, and the industry in general. The company has invested $99 billion in various AI labs, startups, and neo clouds. Plus has announced plans to mobilize over $500 billion in financing for building out AI data centers and other infrastructure. Even before Jensen Huang had resigned, Nvidia was already facing a shareholder lawsuit claiming the company had deceived investors. Jensen Huang and the company’s spokespeople insisted that the relationship with Alice Huang and Megaspeed was “completely normal and not unusual.” Only days later, Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair that raised “national security concerns” without naming anyone specifically. According to Reuters, Jensen Huang misled several Nvidia leaders, “including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld” about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. Many in the AI industry and Silicon Valley jumped to Jensen Huang’s defense. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called it a “sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” in a particularly hyperbolic post. Elon Musk said on X that it would “be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang. Many of Nvidia’s employees even voiced their support to “bring back THE boss,” on an internal post. Some even speculated that Jensen Huang was the victim of a vast conspiracy, whether that was a coup by some faction within Nvidia, or perhaps the goal of China all along had simply been to chase him from the CEO chair. By Thursday night, Reuters reported a third affair, this one also with an Nvidia employee, though no further information has emerged. What happens next First and foremost for Nvidia, it must find a new CEO. It’s possible that Kress eventually ceases to be “interim” CEO, but other names, including Apple’s hardware chief Johny Srouji, have also been rumored. (Donald Trump believes they should hire Tim Cook, but to call that unlikely would be an understatement.) It’s also possible that Nvidia will undergo a dramatic reorganization. Whoever takes over as CEO is unlikely to keep the 60 direct reports of Jensen Huang. With a first-ever board chair in Jones, it’s also possible that the board of directors will play a larger role in the company going forward. The board’s investigation into Jensen Huang that began on November 8th is ongoing. The scandal is likely to drag on for some time. With the possibility that Jensen Huang will have to testify before Congress, the company may choose to be proactive about disclosing any additional information publicly. The incoming Democratic majority is expected to come down harder on Silicon Valley than the current Republican Congress. While it’s unclear just how far the new House and Senate will go in trying to rein in the tech industry and its billionaire leaders, it’s possible it will try to make an example of Nvidia as an early act of strength. If Nvidia is found to have been turning a blind eye to companies like Megaspeed, which are suspected of funneling advanced chips to China, it could face civil or criminal penalties. And it seems increasingly likely that stricter trade restrictions will be implemented on Nvidia’s chips, which could increase tensions with China in an already costly trade war. There is a possibility that Jensen Huang could face criminal charges. In May, he claimed that Nvidia had “zero percent” market share in China due to stringent export restrictions. But shortly after, Culper Research published a report claiming that in reality over 20 percent of the company’s 2026 compute revenue was from China, though that number has not been independently verified. The report cited “illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries” as the primary source of those revenues. Among the largest of those intermediaries, according to Culper Research, was Megaspeed, which Nvidia repeatedly vouched for to the US government. If proof is established that the CEO was knowingly helping Megaspeed or any other companies to illegally divert restricted chips to China, he could face criminal charges. And, as The Verge’s Elizabeth Lopatto put it, “under a functioning legal system, [he] could actually go to jail.” There is the chance that members of the current administration are also tied up in this scandal, as it’s unclear how much the White House knew and when. Considering Nvidia’s sizable investments, borrowing to build data centers, and the importance of its hardware, there are tons of open questions about how this impacts not just the AI industry, but the American economy as a whole. Nvidia is essentially propping up a large part of the tech industry and, if money stops flowing out of its coffers, it could drag a lot of other companies down with it. There are also open questions about how this impacts the American public’s perception of the AI industry. The new Democratic majority was elected in part by campaigning against AI companies and the explosion of data center buildout across the country. That one of its more prominent CEOs is now embroiled in a spying scandal and multiple extramarital affairs probably isn’t going to endear the industry to the public. By the way * Megaspeed was the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia, but when Singaporean newspaper The Straits Times visited its office in October of 2025, it found “no signs of activity.” * Megaspeed is just one of multiple companies that Nvidia has been approved to sell chips with suspicious offices. The New York Times described New Matrix’s headquarters as “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.” * Jensen Huang’s connections to Super Micro are also under scrutiny. Earlier this year, one of its founders, an employee, and a contractor for the company were indicted by the Justice Department for conspiring to violate American export controls and divert Nvidia chips to China. Read this * While a lot has changed, it’s still worth reading the Times’ first big report from October 29th that lays the groundwork for the eventual deluge of international intrigue and infidelity that ultimately led to Jensen Huang’s downfall. * The New York Times paints a fascinating portrait of Alice Huang who now finds herself at the center of an international espionage scandal. * The Decoder interview with Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, digs into what China hoped to get out of Jensen Huang.

articles.title: Fed And OCC Believe Banks Are Strong, But Non-Bank Risks Are Growing
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve’s system-wide evaluation highlights significant private credit and hedge fund vulnerabilities accumulating outside of traditional banks.
articles.body:
The Federal Reserve and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) agree that the banking system is resilient , but the Fed's broader analysis reveals vulnerabilities accumulating outside traditional banking. Private credit vehicles now hold more than $2.6 trillion in financial assets, hedge fund leverage is at its highest level since 2013, and advanced-computing debt issuance has topped $680 billion this year. Together, these trends raise urgent questions about whether interconnected financial exposures are being adequately measured and stress-tested.

Banks currently have strong capital and liquidity positions, profitability has improved, and aggregate credit quality remains relatively sound. That is the reassuring message from two major regulatory assessments released in November 2026: the Federal Reserve's Financial Stability Report and the OCC's Fall 2026 Semiannual Risk Perspective .

The Federal Reserve and the OCC agree that the U.S. banking system remains sound, profitable, and generally well capitalized. But the two agencies examine different parts of the financial landscape. The Federal Reserve tracks vulnerabilities across the entire financial system—including private credit, hedge funds, nonbank financial institutions (NBFIs), market leverage, and cross-market contagion channels. The OCC focuses on the condition and supervisory risks of the national banks and federal savings associations it regulates, including capital, liquidity, loan quality, earnings, cybersecurity, fraud, and operational controls.

The reporting cutoffs also differ. The Federal Reserve's November 2026 report generally reflects information available through October 28, 2026, whereas the OCC's Fall 2026 report primarily reflects data as of June 30, 2026. Because the Fed has a more recent cutoff for market developments, comparisons should account for different dates, definitions, and institution populations.

The following table compares the principal risk categories. "Agreement" means the agencies identify a similar risk or broad condition; it does not mean they use identical measures or reach identical conclusions.

The Banking System: Strong Today, But Not Immune to Shocks

The OCC's bank-performance data are reassuring. First-half 2026 net income reached approximately $116.6 billion, up 23.1% from the first half of 2025 on the back of loan growth, higher net interest and noninterest income, and lower provisions for credit losses. The OCC also reports that cash reserves plus U.S. Treasury holdings represented 17% of total banking-system assets in June 2026, compared with just 4% in June 2008.

articles.title: Bessent, Congress zero in on Lutnick’s role in Nvidia-Megaspeed scandal
articles.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is facing heat in Washington, including from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, over his approach to AI chip export controls amid Nvidia’s national security scandal. Reports emerged this week that Lutnick took a softer line on Nvidia over the tech giant’s AI chip sales to China and failed to put the Singaporean…
articles.body:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is facing heat in Washington, including from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, over his approach to AI chip export controls amid Nvidia’s national security scandal.

Reports emerged this week that Lutnick took a softer line on Nvidia over the tech giant’s AI chip sales to China and failed to put the Singaporean firm Megaspeed on the trade entity blacklist.

Following bipartisan calls to testify, Lutnick has agreed to appear before Congress, but the blame game is already starting with the Trump administration.

“Treasury, War, USTR [U.S. Trade Representative] and State … were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” Bessent said Friday on CNBC’s “Squawk Box.”

“But Commerce has the pen. Commerce BIS has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes,” Bessent added, referring to Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security.

Axios reported Bessent confronted Lutnick last week about the failure to put Megaspeed on Commerce’s entity list , a directory of companies that pose national security risks.

Lutnick said he would “look into it,” while Axios reported the Commerce secretary has been circumventing other administration officials who have sought to tighten the screws on Megaspeed due to its link to China.

Megaspeed is at the center of the Nvidia scandal, an ordeal that led the company’s founder, Jensen Huang, to resign as CEO on Thursday .

Huang admitted last week he had an extramarital affair, and reports indicate it was with Alice Huang, formerly a Megaspeed executive and a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials believe may be a Chinese spy, the New York Times (NYT) reported on Oct. 29.

It is not clear when President Trump, Lutnick or other Commerce officials were informed of the U.S. intelligence community’s suspicions, but Bessent’s comments signal the administration was aware of risks involving Megaspeed.

During his CNBC interview on Friday, Bessent said he and Deputy Treasury Secretary Francis Brooke have “been pushing” for Commerce to add Megaspeed to the entity list “for months.”

“This is a BIS decision,” Bessent noted, after dismissing host Joe Kernen’s suggestion that the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control could take action.

Lawmakers on Capitol Hill are launching probes into the matter and, given Lutnick’s role, sought the Cabinet official’s testimony. The Commerce secretary agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee, chaired by Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), on Dec. 10.

“Recent developments underscore the significant national security and economic interests at stake and the need for timely, substantive engagement with Congress,” Scott wrote in a letter he sent to Lutnick on Thursday.

Democratic Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) cast Lutnick in sharper terms, writing Thursday on the social platform X the Commerce secretary “let the American people down” and put the country’s national security “at risk” by allowing Megaspeed to receive advanced AI chips from Nvidia.

“Lutnick has a lot to answer to,” added Coons, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee who is poised to chair the panel once Democrats take the majority.

Marshall Billingslea, who worked at the Treasury Department during Trump’s first term, noted it is “quite unusual” for Bessent to go public about Cabinet-level discussions about “a matter as sensitive as” the Nvidia-Megaspeed affair.

“To his credit, Scott Bessent & [Secretary of State Marco] Rubio’s team have consistently been right on this topic. Lutnick just ran roughshod over everyone,” Billingslea, the former assistant Treasury secretary for terrorist financing, wrote on X .

He speculated, “I wonder if this means the Commerce Secretary is on his way out?”

In a research note Friday, Beacon Policy Advisors suggested “Lutnick could take the fall, or the administration could push out a lower-ranking official instead” like BIS head Jeffrey Kessler, who, “oversees export controls and does not have the personal relationship with Trump that Lutnick enjoys.”

Earlier this week, the NYT reported Commerce paused its investigation into Megaspeed over whether it helped smuggle Nvidia’s AI chips to China despite U.S. export controls.

Commerce, the NYT reported, passed the probe into Megaspeed off to the Department of Justice (DOJ), due to concerns around Kessler’s handling of the probe. Neither agency confirmed this and the DOJ declined to comment.

While he led Nvidia, Huang faced criticism from lawmakers over his push to sell less advanced chips to China, despite tight export controls. His alliance with Trump helped him successfully lobby the administration to loosen controls and greenlight sales of advanced H200 chips to Beijing last year.

Now, some lawmakers are calling on Lutnick to answer for this shift.

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, and Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.), the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, told Lutnick in a Thursday letter to preserve his department’s records on Trump’s H200 decision.

“There appears to be a profound lack of due diligence in Commerce’s process for approving these Chinese buyers of Nvidia chips,” the lawmakers wrote.

Regardless of Lutnick’s future at the agency, tech analysts are anticipating new policy changes, from Congress and Commerce, as national security concerns remain high.

On Capitol Hill, Huang’s departure is spurring momentum for chip export bills’ inclusion in the annual defense spending bill.

And Commerce “is under pressure to do things,” Beacon Policy Advisors managing partner Stephen Myrow told The Hill.

“On the other hand, they need to make sure whatever they do doesn’t upset the applecart with China that it triggers a renewed export control fight where access to rare earth critical minerals gets supply chained,” he said.

Trump and his Cabinet have walked a delicate line with China amid a tight race on AI development and an intermittent trade war .

The mounting scrutiny on the Trump administration comes as the president prepares to head to China next week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

While there, Trump expects to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, he said last Sunday.

Ian Bremmer, the founder of GZERO Media, said stricter export controls from the federal government in response to the Nvidia-Megaspeed scandal would spark Chinese retaliation and put “pressure” on the relationship between Trump and Xi.

“This is a serious threat to what has been, over the past months, a reasonably warmly managed and very engaged relationship,” Bremmer said in a video . “And it’s not at all clear that can continue even through the remainder of the Trump administration.”

articles.title: Security breaches, tarmac collision exacerbate FAA ground stop aftermath
articles.summary: Security breaches in Denver and Dallas and a tarmac collision in Miami are exacerbating the aftermath of the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) grounding of all flights Friday. The collision at Miami International Airport (MIA) occurred at 9:15 p.m. EST on Saturday when arriving and departing aircrafts made contact with each other at the intersection of…
articles.body:
Security breaches in Denver and Dallas and a tarmac collision in Miami are exacerbating the aftermath of the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) grounding of all flights Friday.

The collision at Miami International Airport (MIA) occurred at 9:15 p.m. EST on Saturday when arriving and departing aircrafts made contact with each other at the intersection of two taxiways, a spokesperson for the airport told The Hill in a statement.

Other flights were diverted to other taxiways to continue airport operations, the spokesperson continued. Two people were treated on the scene of the collision by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue for minor injuries but did not require medical transport.

The collision was similarly confirmed by Copa Airlines — one aircraft company involved — who wrote in a statement on social media , “According to preliminary information, there was a collision between a cargo aircraft and the left wing end of the Boeing 737-800NG while both aircraft were traveling through the airport’s taxiways.”

There was also a security breach at Denver International Airport (DEN) on Saturday evening, and passengers were briefly halted from boarding, according to NewsNation , The Hill’s partner. NewsNation correspondent Nancy Loo reported that DEN officials announced an “operational pause” while she was traveling.

“All gate agents were ordered to stop boarding flights,” she told “NewsNation Prime” by phone. “An audible gasp went through the terminal because everyone was like, ‘No.’ That, on top of everything that’s going on.”

Denver police arrested a man near one of the airport’s security areas for allegedly attempting to breach security at DEN, per NewsNation.

There was another threat on Saturday at Dallas Love Field, per a local NBC affiliate, concerning a security issue involving a commercial aircraft. Police in the area reported there was a threat, but later determined it was unfounded.

The incidents come as nearly 4,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. were delayed as of late Saturday morning, and more than 4,300 were canceled, according to flight tracking website FlightAware , due to a ground stop issued by the FAA on Friday.

“The @FAANews [FAA] issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote on the social platform X . “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”

Systems were back online after Friday, though effects of the historic grounding are still causing delays in some of the country’s busiest airports Sunday.

articles.title: AO3 is back after 17 days.
articles.summary:

It also wants everyone to know that, while some features are temporarily disabled and the site might load a little slowly, your data is still safe:
