articles.title: Trump calls on Congress to fund new air traffic control system
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday asked Congress to fund a new air traffic control system following Friday’s rare nationwide ground stop for all U.S. flights. “If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently. It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World,” the president…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday asked Congress to fund a new air traffic control system following Friday’s rare nationwide ground stop for all U.S. flights.

“If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently. It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post .

“Much of our current air control system is 50 years old – RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve,” he added before pointing blame at the Biden administration, which he said “set it back years.”

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday afternoon issued a ground stop lasting around 4 hours, citing communication issues. The decision is unusual — it’s the third such instance — and disrupted travel throughout the country.

In response, members of the Trump administration and lawmakers have called on Congress to improve what they see as an outdated system.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a Friday night press briefing. “Let’s not do a patchwork, a fix to a system that’s critical for every single family.”

Duffy then asked for $50 billion , adding, “Let’s finish this job: new hardware, new software, new telecommunication.”

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Saturday dismissed any demands for investigation. He instead said in a Fox News interview that “we need further investment.”

“I mean, some of this equipment dates back to the eighties so it’s gotta be updated and that’s our responsibility. We’re gonna work to get it done,” Johnson continued.

The source of the ground stop has not been directly established.

The Transportation Secretary Saturday morning pointed to a telecommunications line switch as the potential cause.

“So what we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router?” he told reporters. “We haven’t determined what the fault was.”

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin rejected concerns that Americans flying were unsafe or that any bad actor was to blame.

“There was no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us,” Mullin told reporters outside of the White House Friday afternoon. “It’s just a telecommunication outage as of right now.”

There was some speculation that the rollout of the FAA’s new AI technology SMART played a part, but Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company which owns SMART, denied involvement .

“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” ASI wrote during the stoppage in a Friday post on X.

articles.title: Fake AI event invites target Microsoft and Google logins
articles.summary: Fake OpenAI event pages promise free ChatGPT Pro subscriptions, then trick employees into handing over Microsoft and Google account credentials.
articles.body: An invitation to an exclusive OpenAI event lands in your inbox. It promises a look at the latest AI tools and even offers three months of ChatGPT Pro for free. All you have to do is register using your work account. Sounds like a pretty good deal, right? Well, before you click that registration button, there's something you should know. Cybercriminals are using fake AI event invitations to trick employees into giving them access to their Microsoft and Google accounts. And some of these attacks can get past the extra security checks many of us rely on. According to a new report from Push Security, attackers have created convincing event registration pages impersonating OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic. Push Security says it detected and blocked visits to the malicious event registration pages on its customers' browsers in late October 2026. The concerning part is how easily an invitation that appears legitimate can lead to someone handing over access to their work account. Here's what researchers discovered and how to protect yourself. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN Fake AI event invites promise free access to premium tools The attackers are taking advantage of the growing interest in artificial intelligence. After all, plenty of employees want to learn how AI can make their jobs easier. A free premium subscription could be enough to get someone's attention. The phishing pages discovered by Push Security promote events that appear to come from recognizable technology companies. One fake OpenAI event advertised a November 4 livestream called "ChatGPT for Social & Digital Marketing Teams." The registration page promised three months of ChatGPT Pro to participants. Another page promoted an invitation-only SpaceX briefing scheduled for November 12. Visitors could supposedly choose between three months of Grok Heavy or a "SpaceX share." Researchers also identified a phishing page impersonating an Anthropic event at AWS re 2026. That page was no longer active when they investigated it. These pages impersonated legitimate technology companies, and the advertised rewards were part of the phishing scheme. Push Security did not suggest that OpenAI, SpaceX or Anthropic operated these fraudulent events. And here's where things get especially concerning. The fake websites tell visitors they must sign in using their corporate Microsoft or Google accounts to complete registration and claim the promised rewards. That request opens the door to the phishing attack. How fake AI event invitations trick employees The criminals have put considerable effort into making these invitations appear credible. Rather than sending people directly to an obvious phishing website, they use familiar online services to help disguise where the links lead. Push Security found that the campaign routed visitors through shortened links associated with Google and Zapier. Earlier related attacks also used legitimate Zoom event pages and GoTo Webinar's email infrastructure. As a result, someone checking an invitation might see a familiar service before reaching the malicious registration page. Researchers have not confirmed the initial delivery method for every invitation in the newer campaign. Once someone reaches the suspicious site, another familiar feature appears. A Cloudflare security challenge asks visitors to confirm they are human. You have probably encountered similar checks while shopping or visiting legitimate websites. However, criminals can use them too. In this campaign, the challenge also made it harder for automated security scanners to examine the malicious pages. After completing the check, visitors arrive at what looks like a professional event registration website. They're presented with two familiar buttons: "Continue with Microsoft" and "Continue with Google." Depending on which button someone selects, the attackers launch a different method designed to capture access to that account. How hackers target Microsoft accounts without a password This is where the attack gets clever. If someone selects "Continue with Microsoft," the phishing website connects to a service called Kali365. It's a phishing-as-a-service platform that criminals can use to carry out account attacks. Kali365 generates a Microsoft device authentication code. The fake registration page then instructs the visitor to copy that code and enter it on Microsoft's legitimate sign-in website. Now, here's why that can fool someone. Microsoft's device authentication process is real. You may have used something similar when connecting a streaming device to an account. However, the attacker started this authentication request. When the victim enters the supplied code and approves the sign-in, Microsoft can issue authentication tokens to the attacker's session. Those tokens may provide access to Microsoft 365 resources without the attacker needing the account password. And the attack may continue from there. Push Security found that the campaign redirects Microsoft users to another phishing service called VoidProxy after the device code step. That second stage attempts to capture their password and authenticated session cookie. A successful compromise could expose company email or documents stored in Microsoft 365. Other connected workplace applications may also be at risk, depending on the permissions and access associated with the compromised account. How the Google phishing attack steals login sessions The Google option takes another approach. When visitors click "Continue with Google," the phishing page opens a pop-up that appears to contain Google's familiar sign-in screen. However, that login process runs through VoidProxy, which acts as an intermediary between the person signing in and Google's actual authentication service. As someone enters their credentials, the phishing service can capture the information. It can also intercept certain multifactor authentication responses and steal session cookies. So, what exactly is a session cookie? Think of it as a digital pass that helps a website remember you've already signed in. Once your identity has been verified, that cookie can allow you to continue using your account without entering your password on every page. If a criminal obtains a usable session cookie, they may be able to reuse that authenticated session and gain access without completing the usual login process again. That's why these attacks are particularly dangerous for people who believe that enabling multifactor authentication automatically protects them from every account takeover attempt. It's important to note that Push Security documented the malicious infrastructure and blocked visits to the phishing pages. Its report did not establish how many accounts, if any, were successfully compromised through this campaign. HACKERS HIDE DANGEROUS FAKE AI DOWNLOADS BEHIND GOOGLE ADS Why these fake AI event scams are difficult to spot The attackers are combining two phishing services behind the same registration pages. Kali365 targets Microsoft's device authentication process, while VoidProxy targets authenticated login sessions. Meanwhile, the fake event websites borrow the appearance of familiar brands. The criminals can also change their websites and event themes as older pages get discovered. Researchers also discovered that the fraudulent registration pages could automatically display content in a visitor's language.
